speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do wish to speak on this Bill, and I am glad to have the chance today. This is a Bill to privatize Eldorado Nuclear Limited, a small firm renamed and taken over by the Government in 1942. Since then it has been the recipient of a vast amount of government subsidies. The Government has pumped taxpayers' money into this firm. In spite of that, the firm still has debts which the Government is willing to pay off as a favour to any prospective buyer.
It is a bad deal, financially, but there is another aspect that is even worse that I will address shortly. First, I wish to review the generally bad aspects of the deal. This deal is arranged in such a manner that the public sector will be taking the debts, while the private sector takes the profits. This is what is traditionally known as socialism for the rich. Many corporations that will indirectly benefit from this, and many individuals who will directly benefit from this, pay no tax. We do not know exactly who until the time comes, but we do know that they will be among those rich people in Canada who pay no tax, and they will be subsidized by the working people, small business people, and farmers of Canada who pay taxes. As I said, large multimillion dollar debts of this company will be taken over by the Government after the agreement to sell this company to private owners for their private profit. That is one problem.
Another problem is that the safety regulations, which have not been enforced as well as they ought to be in the case of a public corporation, will be much less enforced in the case of a private corporation. I am speaking of safety to the workers, safety to the neighbouring public, and safety to the environment. The sale of this company into private hands will put the industry in the position of becoming a much greater physical risk to those who work there, to those who live nearby, and to the air, water, and soil of our country. Those are the general problems.
What I want to speak of particularly is that this company, Eldorado, has been from the outset part of a scam. I am not referring only to the cartel for price fixing, of which it was part and on which the evidence was gathered by the Department of Justice; 75,000 documents of evidence gathered and kept secret until this day. Nevertheless, clearly there is no question that Eldorado and other companies in the cartel, Canadian and international, were guilty of price fixing. The matter was never brought to court, because Eldorado during this time has been a Crown corporation and was therefore able to misuse or to abuse the royal prerogative to avoid being sued for its violation

April 15, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
of the laws of Canada. I am speaking of a still more serious scam, and that is a scam in the relationship between nuclear power and nuclear weapons.
I refer partly to an address recorded in The Gazette for April 14, 1988 by Helen Caldicott who says to us through the audience she addressed in Montreal:
You are the root of half the arsenal of nuclear bombs in the world.
This is what she told her audience of about 900 people at St. Patrick's Church in Montreal. She goes on to say that if we continue with the proposed nuclear powered subs, we will be extending our guilt for the proliferation of the threat of nuclear devastation either by accident or by war.
What happened was that in the 1940s Canada helped the United States to build the atomic bombs that were tested in the U.S., mostly on non-humans, not deliberately on humans though some American and some Canadian soldiers have suffered severely from the radiation to which they were exposed there, but they were tested cold-bloodedly on the people of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Canada helped by providing uranium and by providing expertise. This was done primarily through Eldorado. Canada for many years, then, has sold uranium to the United States.
When the United States uranium industry became protectionist and objected to the importing of Canadian uranium, the Canadian Government under Lester Pearson became more peace loving and said: "We won't sell uranium except for peaceful purposes". They never explained from that date to this how you identify a uranium atom or a uranium molecule or a uranium shipment, for that matter, when it has been stockpiled with uranium from other mines, or how you tell which one was used for peaceful purposes only and which one was used to produce weapons grade plutonium for bombs.
At the time this scam was promoted by Eisenhower, the former General commanding U.S. Forces in Europe and later recycled as President of Columbia University and then as President of the United States. In 1953, when Eisenhower spoke to the United Nations General Assembly, he undertook to announce a new nuclear policy for the U.S. He proposed, and I quote, "to take this weapon out of the hands of the soldiers and put it into the hands of those who will know how to strip its military casing and adapt it to the arts of peace". He was going to establish a new international agency called "Atoms for Peace". They were going to provide abundant electrical power, growing roses in the Antarctic, and so on and so forth. It was quite a paradise that he described. He assured us that this Atoms for Peace would "diminish the potential destructive power of the world's atomic stockpiles", and a further quote that they would be "entirely eliminating the use of atomic energy for destructive purposes and promoting its use for industrial and humanitarian purposes".
Canada, through Eldorado, went along with this project disguised as a pipe-dream for Utopia with cheap, safe power. Canada helped to set up the International Atomic Energy
Agency, which facilitated the sale of uranium and overlooked the serious dangers of uranium from Canada and other uranium producing countries being used to produce nuclear weapons.
During these years Canada prided itself on not manufacturing or storing nuclear weapons, except for a few years when we had the Bomarc nuclear warhead here. Some Canadians were making plenty of money. Other Canadians were subsidizing the industry from the beginning, but the owners of uranium industries were making plenty of money by selling uranium to the United States and to other bomb-producing countries, including even the Soviet Union.
There was also the project of producing the CANDU reactor. The CANDU was a flop commercially. It has had to be constantly subsidized by the taxpayers; again the profits go mainly to the owners directly or indirectly, to the financiers, to the banks and others that lend the money to this money losing, weapons producing industry. I call it "weapons producing" because even though no Canadian agency has manufactured the bombs, we have been an important part of the American bomb manufacturing industry.
This has been well documented in a book called Canada and the Nuclear Arms Race, particularly a section by Gordon Edwards, a professor of mathematics, called "Canada's Nuclear Industry and the Myth of the Peaceful Atom". He points out that when, for example, there was concern about proliferation of nuclear weaponry into Argentina through the use of Canada's CANDU reactor and materials associated with it, there was a high level discussion and there was an inquiry, not a public inquiry but a judiciously private inquiry. The nuclear review was carried out by an interdepartmental committee of

Mr. Speaker, I am taking part in this debate because I feel that from now until June, the Government will use delaying tactics of this kind to put an end to debates in the House, to shorten them, and perhaps even to silence some opposition Members who would like to speak on certain subjects.
I will remind Hon. Members that yesterday in the House, I raised a series of issues that the Government must address, subjects as important as the privatization of Air Canada and
April 15, 1988

abortion. So the Government must present the legislation as soon as possible if we are to study these issues seriously in the House by the end of June.

In speaking to the motion before us, which motion is that the question be now put, I would like to state that the Liberal caucus does not like this tactic of the Government. Nevertheless, it has been done now. We hope that the Government will not make a habit of it and will allow for the exercise of free speech without having to go to such extremes.
Bill C-121, an Act to authorize the reorganization and divestiture of Eldorado Nuclear Limited and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, with reservations from the Liberal caucus, will receive our affirmative vote. That is the case basically because this Bill seems to be a step in the right direction, and we favour the move.
I must tell Hon. Members that for political reasons and from a political perspective I personally may have some difficulties with this merger. It is a gift to Premier Grant Devine and his Saskatchewan buddies. I am not very inclined at this time to be very nice to Mr. Devine because he is not being very nice to me. Therefore with that reservation, a personal one, and without putting that reservation before my vote, I will stand in my place to support the Bill. I hope that Premier Devine will do the same in his province, stand up and support some of the things for which we all fight, that is, basic fundamental rights in Canada, and give generously to his people.
The assets of Eldorado are valued at about $915.9 million while the assets of Saskatchewan Mining and Development Corporation, which is the company with which Eldorado will be merged, are $973.2 million. The Government of Canada will have a 38.5 per cent share of the new company while Saskatchewan will have a 61.5 per cent share.
The new company will issue promissory notes valued at 40 per cent of fixed assets to cover all the debt owed to the Saskatchewan Government, and $230 million of the $570 million owed to the Government of Canada.
It is indeed a gift to the Province of Saskatchewan. We are covering the debt by doing this and helping Saskatchewan balance its books. However, the price for which the Government of Canada is selling Eldorado nevertheless appears low to some of us.
Some stock brokerage companies, in particular Burns Fry, which is assisting the Government with this sale, has explained to us some of the difficulties of placing a value on the Saskatchewan Mining and Development Corporation and Eldorado Nuclear, which is a federally owned company. The two companies were evaluated from a discounted cash flow basis rather than from an assets basis. SMDC had lower operating costs, partially as a result of lower royalties. Eldorado was also determined to be lower in value as a result of its less profitable refinery business.
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
We know that the product that the Canadian uranium industry exports makes Canada one of the leading producers and exporters of uranium. I have statistics with which I will not bore the House but which state that in 1987 Canadian output and exports each exceeded 12,000 tonnes of uranium, surpassing the five year highs set in 1986. The value of Canadian uranium production exceeded $1 billion in 1987.
One of the points that I would like to touch upon in the few minutes available to me is that the head office of the new merged company will be moved to Saskatchewan. This means that there will be 50 employees who will be without jobs. However, if we are to believe some of the press reports, there will be some efforts made by the new merged privatized company to look very attentively at the possibility of offering to these people future employment if at all possible. I hope that they will be treated fairly and justly and that they will not suffer from this decision and from this transfer to Saskatchewan.
I hope that if among these employees there are francophones, they will be able to go to Saskatchewan, have their kids educated in Saskatchewan en franqais, s'il vous plait, and have access to their courts as well as access to the legislature, in French as well as in English because of course that is a fact of life in Saskatchewan.
Having made these few remarks I would like to say to the House once again that we indeed support Bill C-121. I do not think that we have any further speakers on it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in the New Democratic Party oppose the sale of Eldorado Nuclear Limited because in our opinion it is a bad deal. It is a bad deal for Canadians. I have a whole number of concerns. I have listened to the speeches over the last several days on this Bill. I think anyone watching this debate will readily recognize that there are many facets to what the Government is attempting to do here. One of those with which I have a great deal of concern is the environmental implications of this deal.
Considering the environmental aspects of Bill C-121 I think a greater consideration should be given to the situation of Eldorado Nuclear now and the wider implications of uranium mining which the new merged company will encounter. Eldorado Nuclear has severe environmental problems with which to deal, especially at its Port Hope, Ontario, refinery, and at its northern Saskatchewan mine sites. Essentially the Eldorado Port Hope dump site is full.
The situation has been summarized this way by research staff from the Library of Parliament. The researchers have pointed out that the effluent treatment process at the Port Hope refinery produces approximately 600 tonnes per year of solid waste which is mainly calcium oxide containing calcium fluoride and uranium at 500 to 1000 parts per thousand.
This material and much smaller quantities of other smaller wastes that contain metallic impurities, including arsenic, are dumped at a licensed site near Port Hope, the Granby dump

April 15, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
site. This depository is close to being full and yet no alternate site or plan has been selected. Eldorado has been waiting for the federal Government to decide what should be done with this dump, and presumably the new company will also wait for direction.
Any plan that requires the removal of the material to a new site will be very expensive, mainly in terms of transportation, and according to the details released with the merger plans, the costs, possibly up to as much as $100 million, will be borne mainly by the federal Government.
That is according to the research staff of the Parliamentary Library, and I think all Hon. Members have a great respect for the integrity of the research done by the staff in the research branch.
The resolution of Port Hope is mainly to dump the responsibility onto the federal Government which will pay the bulk of the costs. In our estimation, the first $2 million will be borne by the company and the next $98 million or 23.5 per cent will be borne by the company, with 76.5 per cent of the cost being borne by the federal Government. Any cost above $100 million will be borne entirely by the federal Government. I defy anyone to say that that is a good deal for the taxpayers of Canada who will end up absorbing these costs.
Why is there such a sweetheart deal for a company being purchased as it is? Companies are normally purchased with assets and liabilities, but some of the key liabilities in this transaction have been taken over by the federal Government. We must ask why this is so. The answer is simply that the Government is desperately anxious for a good share price on the flotation of the new company's stock. What better way to achieve that than for the federal Government to assume the liability of environmental responsibilities and Eldorado's enormous debt?
Eldorado's environmental difficulties do not end with the dump sites. There are further problems in Port Hope and in Saskatchewan's mine mills. Again, according to the researchers from the Library of Parliament, the continued operation of the Port Hope facility, especially at present high rates of production, will generate considerable levels of solid and liquid waste. With the proximity of the plant to both Lake Ontario and the town site, the new company would do its image a great deal of good by committing itself to efforts to recycle or clean up and sell all such wastes. No mention has been made of such an approach, according to the researchers.
Clean-up problems exist at the mills in Saskatchewan as well. The tailings that are produced contain small amounts of uranium, radium and other elements. Very good effluent treatment is required on an ongoing basis, and a thorough understanding of the principles involved have to be taught to the personnel involved. Historically, such understanding has been suspect at best.
The two areas I have just pointed out have been identified as problems which the Government has yet to acknowledge. This leads to the suspicion that the Government feels that the less said about environmental aspects of uranium production, the better. This is unfortunate for a Government that assumed office with some expectations that it would examine the inherent difficulties of the nuclear fuel cycle.
Although there is considerable public support for such an inquiry, there has not been one. We in the New Democratic Party have formed our own inquiry headed by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) and the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell).
At this time when the Government is backing away from involvement with uranium, it would be an appropriate time to review the issues involved with uranium mining, particularly in light of recent experience in Canada where new high-grade ore mines have developed in recent years and are likely to require both novel and sophisticated technologies. Similarly, Atomic Energy control regulations have been under review for a number of years. A public inquiry could reveal the problems of mining uranium at this time.
I think this issue begs that I ask some of the environmental questions associated with uranium mining which are grouped around three themes: occupational safety for miners, public health hazards from mine waste and disposal and the propriety of producing material for possible use in nuclear weapons.
As I pointed out earlier, the New Democratic Party opposes this deal because it is a bad deal. It is a bad deal on environmental grounds and it is certainly a bad deal for the taxpayers of Canada. I say that because the deal is structured so that the public sector takes the risks and obligations and the private sector gets the profits, profits not only from the commercial activities of the company merged from Eldorado and the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation but also from the heavy public subsidies which are given the uranium mining industry in the form of favourable taxation, marketing arrangements and sweetheart contracts.
The House has been given no assurances from the Government that it recognizes the sacrifice of the public sector and the public interest in this deal. It is clear that this deal has been structured so that the Government can say that privatization works, just look at the share price. However, of all sectors of industry, I cannot think of another that is less appropriate for privatization than the nuclear industry. In my opinion, it displays an ideological approach that defies any kind of logic or responsibility to the public which is supposed to be represented by the Government.
In order for this stock flotation deal to succeed, and that is all it really is, the public sector will underwrite the risks by assuming the debt of Eldorado Nuclear and Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation and the federal Government will assume the further liability of Eldorado's nuclear waste problems at Port Hope at a cost of perhaps some $75 million. This take-back of debt has been described by the financial
April 15, 1988

advisers to the Government, Burns Fry, another respected organization, as being necessary for the flotation. Eldorado's debts are substantial. They are in the range of $550 million.
The federal Government will receive from the newly merged company about $250 million, leaving $300 million that must be made up in the sale of shares in the new company before the Government breaks even on its debt obligations alone. This is to say nothing of the cumulative investment which has been made in Eldorado in the form of government equity.
The Government needs a high share price or else it will wind up with a brick in its hands, or something like a BCRIC, the B.C. resource privatization under the Bennett Government which issued shares at $5, shares which now trade for about 80 cents or 90 cents.
There are a whole number of concerns to which the Government has not responded in the House in its defence of this Bill. I am rather disappointed that more Members from the government side have not spoken out on behalf of their own constituents' interest in this matter. I am sure the concerns I have expressed are shared by many Canadians, regardless of where they live in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in the debate on this very important piece of legislation. My colleague from Beaches has set out in his usual eloquent manner a number of reasons, both environmental and financial, for our opposition to this legislation. He has noted that government Members seem somewhat reluctant to defend this provision, and I am saddened as well to note that the Official Opposition seems to be supporting this legislation. Indeed, I suppose that this is not terribly surprising because too often we have seen that the initial suggestion for other privatization ventures by this Government came from the Liberal Party of Canada.
We know that the Conservative Government, in its obsession with the private sector and its contempt for a strong and vibrant public sector accountable to the people of Canada, is now in the process of selling off, in a sense, Canada's heritage as a nation. I speak of Crown corporations such as Air Canada where we had the announcement earlier this week that the Conservative Government intends to sell it off. We have put the Government on notice that we will do everything in our power to block this sale, which is not only wrong in principle but which is opposed by the great majority of Canadians from coast to coast.
I would point out that among those who oppose the sale of Air Canada are federal Progressive Conservative supporters. A majority of them are saying to their Government: Back off. Air Canada is running well. We are concerned that smaller communities should not be denied effective transportation and if it is privatized, then there is a real risk that both service and safety will deteriorate.
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
I mentioned the fact that, sadly, it was the Liberal Party that started this trend towards privatization. Indeed, it was the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), then Minister of Transport, who suggested, I believe in March of 1984, that the time had come to privatize Air Canada. However, not only will we in the NDP do everything in our power to block the sale of this vital Crown corporation, we have also said that following the next federal election an NDP Government will take Air Canada back into public hands. That is our commitment to the people of Canada.
We approached this legislation with deep concern from a number of perspectives, including environmental and sound financial management, from the perspective of those who work in the industry, and certainly from the perspective of a movement which has historically argued for a strong public sector, particularly in essential areas of the economy. Let us not forget that it was in the 1940s that the federal Government recognized the importance of nuclear energy by first expropriating the assets of Eldorado Mines and then using the declaratory power in the then British North America Act to take jurisdiction over this resource. It was precisely that action which underlined the seriousness with which nuclear energy was regarded and certainly should still be regarded.
We as New Democrats also believe we must break the cycle of nuclear proliferation. The risks inherent in continued nuclear proliferation at all stages are very great. My colleague from Beaches spoke of the concern over nuclear wastes and the fact that the Port Hope facility is almost full. As a society we still have not come up with a method for safely disposing of nuclear wastes.
As well, we are concerned about the health of those who work in the industry. There are serious occupational health and safety concerns that arise. That is partly why two of the major unions who represent workers at Eldorado and Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation are fundamentally opposed to this legislation. I am speaking of the Energy and Chemical Workers Union that represents employees at the Cluff Lake Mine in northern Saskatchewan in which SMDC holds a majority share, and the United Steelworkers, who represent employees at the Key Lake Mine, the Rabbit Lake Mine, and three locals of the Eldorado uranium refinery at Port Hope. Those people who work in the field are asking the Government to back off on its ideological obsession with privatization, with paying off its friends in the private sector.
We say that this matter is of concern on environmental grounds also. We say it is a concern to the workers. We also say it is a bad deal economically. Why? Because the deal is structured in such a way that the public sector takes all of the real risks and obligations, and the private sector gets the profits. It is the same old story that Tommy Douglas used to tell so effectively, and we are seeing it again in this legislation. For example, we have just learned, I believe it was in this morning's Globe and Mail, that the profits of SMDC have doubled. The company recorded a $60.3 million profit in 1987, almost double what it made the previous year. What is

April 15, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
happening to that company? It is being sold off to the private sector.
I am a Member of Parliament from British Columbia and I remember a similar sale of public assets by the British Columbia Resources Investment Corporation. I remember the Premier of British Columbia telling us that this was an example of private enterprise at work, of the market system at its finest. If that is an example of the market system at its finest, God help us, because it was a disaster for the ordinary people of British Columbia who, after all, owned all of the assets in those corporations in the first place.

Mr. Speaker, we in the NDP support a large public sector in Canada. For example, we called for the nationalization of a Canadian bank. This would allow us some influence on the banks' policies throughout Canada. It would also allow us to exert greater influence on financial policies in Canada. This is not a very radical policy. All, or almost all, countries in the western world, including France, Italy, West Germany, Belgium and many others, have a public stake in the financial sector.
And I take this opportunity to correct the suggestion made in an article in today's La Presse by Mario Fontaine, who suggests that the NDP's policy is to nationalize all the banks in Canada. That is not at all the case, Mr. Speaker, but we are in favor of nationalizing one bank, as many other countries in the world have already done.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have the opportunity that the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) gave me to speak again. I appreciate that very much. I hope he continues to use that kind of strategy and tactic in the conduct of the business of the House.
We in the NDP have no problem with the merging of two Crown corporations, Eldorado Nuclear and the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation. Eldorado is mainly in the refining end of the business with some mining, and SMDC is in the mining business in the main. However, the Government then says it will privatize that merged company and turn it over to private investors via the stock market. With the shape which the stockmarket is in, this is perhaps a stupid time to be making share offerings for Eldorado and Air Canada which would amount to something in the order of $400 million to $500 million. The offering will either fail or the shares will go for a pittance, which means that the taxpayers are again taken to the cleaners.
I would like to point out another example of the poor treatment which the taxpayers get at the hands of the Government. The people of Canada invested hundreds of millions of dollars in Eldorado. The people of Saskatchewan probably invested hundreds of millions of dollars in the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation.
We all know that over the last number of years the uranium market has been soft, to put it mildly. In fact, prices were down so badly that we could hardly give the stuff away. However, things have improved. As was reported in today's Globe and Mail, the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation had a net profit last year of $60.3 million, double the profit of the year before, and it reduced its long-term debt from $600 million to around $315 million over the last three or four years. However, it still has long-term debts in excess of $300 million. Eldorado Nuclear has debts of about $300 million.
The pattern is the same in the case of the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation. Every time the taxpayers get a chance to get a return on their investment, or to get their money back, the free enterprise nonsense comes out from under the rocks, the Tories come out of the woodwork and say that because it is making a profit it should be sold to their private enterprise friends.
You cannot win with the Tories. If a Crown corporation loses money, ergo Crown corporations are bad in principle and in general. They are terrible, they do not work, they are inefficient, et cetera. If a Crown corporation makes a profit, it is equally bad, according to the Tories. The Government and the taxpayers have no business being in an enterprise which should be in the hands of the private sector. You cannot win with these birds.
That kind of convoluted thinking and double standard set out by the Government over nearly the last four years cause many people to believe that the Government does not know what it is doing, that it does not know what it wants to do or how it wants to do it. The only thing the Government has been consistent about is the narrow ideological binge that it is on in this case, the case of Air Canada, and a number of other matters.
In addition to being taken again by the privatization of a company which will be making a profit and being denied a chance to get a return on their investment or to get their money back, this Bill saddles the taxpayers with $300 million of the debt of Eldorado Nuclear. That is not the first time the Government has done that. You and I, Mr. Speaker, could be good capitalists and free enterprisers too if someone would offer us a company on the cheap without any of the debts and all of the assets.
Why should the taxpayer be victimized by the Government's headlong plunge into turning an industry over to the private sector when the long-term future of the investment is good and
April 15, 1988

the opportunity exists for the taxpayers to get their money back and maybe even make a profit on it? The Conservatives want the taxpayer to pay both ways.
If you were in the private sector and went to the stock exchange in Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal or New York and announced a share offering in a private company, announcing as well that you were going to keep a majority interest in the company and instruct your members of the board of directors to vote with the minority private shareholders, they would laugh you out of the place. You would not be able to give a share away.
However, that is the methodology of the Tories in their announcement about Air Canada. If the Government sells 45 per cent of the shares of the company to the private sector it still retains, on behalf of the taxpayers, 55 per cent of the ownership of Air Canada. The Minister says that the Government will instruct the government members on the board of directors to vote the majority stock with the minority stockholders. If you were to do that in a private company you would be fired the next day. No group of a majority of shareholders would hold still for that kind of nonsense.
However, that is the way the Government is treating the taxpayers. We think that the deal itself and the way the public is being treated by the Government is so fundamentally bad that the Bill should be withdrawn. The Bill should go back to the drawing board. Those two Crown corporations should simply be merged into one and the taxpayers should be given an opportunity to get their money back.

Mr. Speaker, I should think not. I know that you yourself have quite enjoyed the debate that has been entered into with particular vigour over the last couple of days on a matter of increasingly obvious importance. I am sure that you enjoyed our examination yesterday of the ideological basis of this legislation which would merge the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation and Eldorado Nuclear. I am sorry to see that the Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) is not here to continue the exploration of the faults underlying this Bill.
Yesterday we said that this Bill was a very nice example of the triumphs of ideology in that Eldorado Nuclear dramatized many of the difficulties and the failures of the Government to consider all of the ramifications of actions that it takes under the umbrella of ideology.

RADIO-CANADA IMPORTANCE OF RETAINING ANIMATION BRANCH
speechtext:

We must not forget that most of the international recognition received by Radio-Canada in the past was based on the quality of the productions of its animation department. We see here one of the disastrous results of the Government's budget cuts in cultural affairs.

Frederic Back and his colleagues in the animation department at Radio-Canada have won two Oscars in six years. I call on the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) to start funding the CBC in such a way that future generations of

April 15, 1988
Canadian artists will have the opportunity to match Mr. Back's achievement.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are becoming more and more convinced that the present Government is providing good government.
Canadians have sifted through the rhetoric of the NDP and have found it lacking in substance. Canadians see an Official Opposition devoid of policies and direction, and we are watching a Liberal Government in Ontario increase spending by 10 per cent per year while in good economic times. It has even threatened higher taxes in its upcoming budget.
This Government's record of job creation is unprecedented. The unemployment rate in Ontario is at its lowest in 14 years. Canadians are saying that they do not want to return to double digit inflation, double digit interest rates, a double digit unemployment rate, and runaway deficits. Canadians want good government and they are getting it.

subtopic: SASKATCHEWAN LANGUAGE BILL-POSITION OF QUEBEC PREMIER

speechtext:
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, how can Premier Bourassa of Quebec condone Saskatchewan Bill 2 when every language minority group in the country says that this Bill is a step backward for language justice? Is it because Premier Bourassa wants to hand out similar treatment to the anglophone minority in Quebec once the Supreme Court renders its judgment on bilingual signs under Quebec Bill 101?
Saskatchewan Bill 2 cuts back on francophone rights which the Supreme Court of Canada said existed in Saskatchewan prior to 1905, and the sign provisions of Bill 101 cut back on rights held by Quebec Anglophones for over 100 years. Both measures are contrary to the spirit of the Canadian Constitution, the Meech Accord, and federal Bill C-72.
In these circumstances, I urge Premier Bourassa and Devine to adopt a spirit of tolerance, generosity, and fairness with respect to their language minorities and to amend their language Bills accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday's announcement by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) concerning the establishment of review committees for federal judicial appointments is another step in the right direction toward an open and public appointments process. As you know, appointments to federal boards and agencies have been subject to a parliamentary review for almost three years now.
Unfortunately, the same cannot be said for the Province of Ontario where Premier David Peterson has rejected a recommendation signed by some of his own Liberal members of the Legislature calling for the establishment of a similar review process for appointments to provincial boards and agencies. Instead, Premier Peterson has opted to consult opposition Party Leaders in private in connection with only a few appointments.
What we need at all levels of government is not a secret process but an open one; a process in which all positions are publicly advertised and applied for, and where all positions are subject to a parliamentary review.

subtopic: PRISON INMATE'S HALFWAY HOUSE APPLICATION DENIED
PRISON INMATE'S HALFWAY HOUSE APPLICATION DENIED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak out on a grave injustice which has been done to the son of a couple who live in my constituency in Burnaby. His name is Sonny McLaren. He is a man who has served over 12 years on a sentence of 61-1/2 years for breaking into a Masonic lodge in the United States, with no injury involved, and stealing less than $100.
As I say, he served over 12 years. Recently, though, he has had solid support from correction officials and parole officers and from his family to move into a halfway house in Vancouver, operated by the Salvation Army. Yesterday, the National Parole Board dashed Sonny McLaren's hopes. He has been treated in an appalling fashion by the National Parole Board. It ignored all of the recommendations of those who have been working with him.
This is the same National Parole Board that lets out a Foster but keeps in a Sonny McLaren. I say shame on the National Parole Board for its treatment of Sonny McLaren in these circumstances.
I call on Ole Ingstrup, Chairman of the National Parole Board, to review this cruel decision very quickly and to grant Sonny McLaren's appeal in order to allow him to get on with his life.
April 15, 1988

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO WORK OF CIVIL AVIATION TRIBUNAL
TRIBUTE TO WORK OF CIVIL AVIATION TRIBUNAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the mandate of the Civil Aviation Tribunal established June 1, 1986, pursuant to the recommendations of the Dubin inquiry into aviation safety in Canada, is to provide the aviation community with an independent appeal system with regard to enforcement decisions and penalties assessed by the Ministry of Transport under the Aeronautics Act.
The Tribunal is now bringing natural justice to aviation matters. Under the chairmanship of Mr. J. W. Snow, the Tribunal has done an excellent job disposing of some 127 cases in 1987, its first full year of operation. Both the aviation fraternity and the Ministry of Transport are served well by this independent tribunal.

Mr. Speaker, this weekend a group of Guatemalan nationals will be returning to their country for the first time. These are a group of individuals who have valiantly fought for the cause of human rights in their own country. In the last several years they have been forced into exile and have been speaking and trying to interest other countries in the plight of their colleagues and friends in their own country.
This weekend they will be returning for the first time to give test to the new Guatemalan Government's commitment to open up human rights and provide for a more beneficial environment. They will be accompanied by a group of international observers, including a clergyman from Canada. 1 think it is essential that other countries take note of this very important action both as a way of providing protection and also giving testimony to their valiant and courageous act.
I call upon our Department of External Affairs to ensure that the observation monitoring of our own Department will be carefully directed toward Guatemala this weekend, and it may want to contact the Guatemalan Government. Most important, I hope Members of this House will not only recognize the importance of this act of courage but also lend their support to this very initiative.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for many years the Liberals appointed judges on a strictly partisan basis, almost like the Senate. Yesterday, our Government and our Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) put an end to this system of partisan appointments.
This Government is not only cleaning up patronage but also changing the system, so that once and for all on Parliament Hill, procedures will be open and crystal clear, so that competence will be the only basis for selection.
Under the Conservatives, Mr. Speaker, integrity is gaining ground on Parliament Hill.
* *
*

Mr. Speaker, last night on the evening shift at Canada Post's Alta Vista Terminal in Ottawa, 50 to 75 unionized workers were suspended. According to some reports, more than 90 per cent of the women on the shift were suspended. For the most part these women were suspended for having their purses in the work area.
Canada Post says it is doing this to protect the security of the mail. It already had the right to search purses of people entering or leaving the workplace. It already had the right to search lockers. The difference is that in the Marchment report that looked at the Post Office, Judge Marchment said people should only be searched if there were reasonable grounds to believe something was wrong.
The Post Office has gone much further. One woman was suspended because she wanted to keep her purse with medication in it. One man was suspended because he had a sports paper in his back pocket. One man was suspended for not putting his jacket in his locker even though, according to witnesses, the man had not been issued a locker.
The Post Office is being stupid and provocative. It already has the tools to deal with security. What it is trying to do is pick a fight with the union and abuse the workers. This is not the way to build a better Post Office.

April 15, 1988

Mr. Speaker, for the past few days the Canada-Europe Parliamentary Association has been hosting a delegation from the Western European Union which consists of members of the national Parliaments of Germany, Luxembourg, France, Belgium, Italy, Netherlands, Portugal, and the United Kingdom. The members of this very important group of European countries are most interested in our mutual defence, arms limitation, and other similar topics which impinge on the NATO alliance and on our countries individually.
These are our colleagues. These are our friends. These are our allies. In fact, most members of this House can trace their heritage to one of these countries.
I want to emphasize the policy of our Government that we will remain in NATO, that we will continue to enhance our presence in the alliance in Europe with men and material. To do less, to weaken our resolve in any way, would be to betray our friends, our colleagues, our allies, our forefathers. This we will not do.

Mr. Speaker, I read with absolute shock and dismay the latest in the series of actions taken by the Premier of British Columbia who claims to be in support of the family. With his latest decision to cut off welfare for single mothers who have one child over the age of three and one-half months, or have two children under the age of 12 years, he is penalizing the children of this country.
The federal Government, through its CAP funding, does much to support welfare programs in various provinces. I call upon the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) to show some leadership in this area, to contact the Premier of British Columbia and tell him that this latest action is completely unacceptable. It is going to hurt the children of British Columbia and, what is more, if the Minister stands by silently and lets this happen, it is going to be hurtful to the children and the families of Canada.

subtopic: GEORGES BANK-GRANTING OF NEW OFFSHORE LOBSTER FISHING LICENCES OPPOSED
GEORGES BANK-GRANTING OF NEW OFFSHORE LOBSTER FISHING LICENCES OPPOSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 1 the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon)
issued four new offshore lobster licences giving access to the lobster grounds on Georges Bank. This decision has been widely criticized by the provincial Legislature, the inshore lobster fishermen, the community in general, and by this Member of Parliament.
The Minister must realize that the fishing industry is serious business in western Nova Scotia and my constituents do not take lightly to having decisions imposed upon them. The message from my constituents is very clear. The issuing of new offshore lobster licences was unacceptable in the past, and nothing has changed to make the decision acceptable. On this issue, I stand with my fishermen.

subtopic: ISRAEL-REPORTED USE OF TOXIC GASES AGAINST PALESTINIAN DEMONSTRATORS
ISRAEL-REPORTED USE OF TOXIC GASES AGAINST PALESTINIAN DEMONSTRATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in recent days there have been reports that Israeli forces may be using highly toxic gases in their efforts to control Palestinian demonstrations in the occupied territories. These gases are reported to cause severe abdominal pain and impaired muscle control, to cause miscarriages and even death. If these reports are accurate, the use of toxic gases represents a frightening development in the ongoing violence in the occupied territories and should be condemned by all Members of this House and, indeed, the entire world community.
Just as Canadians are outraged at the use of chemical weapons in the Iran-Iraq war, so should we be outraged if these most recent reports are true. The use of chemical weapons by any nation is morally abhorrent and has absolutely no place in a civilized world.
I urge the Government to endeavour vigorously to determine the accuracy of the recent reports and, if they are true, to speak out forcefully against the use of chemical weapons against Palestinians, or anyone else for that matter.

Mr. Speaker, I was delighted with the announcement of the Government that Revenue Canada will carry into effect administrative measures and amendments to the Income Tax Act to expedite tax credit refunds for qualified Canadian controlled private corporations engaged in scientific research. The R and D tax credit provides assistance for corporations in those years in which they do not have any tax liability. This program has already stimulated over $1 billion of research activity in Canada.
April 15, 1988

The Government will issue refunds or partial refunds for R and D claims made by Canadian controlled private corporations, with established track records as research and development performers, within two months of their filing complete claims with the Department, in other words, prior to an audit of those companies. This will ensure that companies with a proven track record in R and D do not experience administrative delays in the processing of tax refunds.
These tax improvements will assist the cash flow of small firms and enable them to plan their long-term activities better. The announced tax amendments will mean a more stable research and development sector, more jobs for highly qualified Canadians, and a more competitive economy.

subtopic: UNITED STATES OMNIBUS TRADE BILL-APPLICATION OF COUNTERVAIL MEASURES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: UNITED STATES OMNIBUS TRADE BILL-APPLICATION OF COUNTERVAIL MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question would have been directed to the Minister for International Trade, but in his absence I will put the question to the Deputy Prime Minister. On April 3, 1987, the Prime Minister of Canada told the Wall Street Journal. "Trade remedy laws can't apply to Canada. You can't have a free trade arrangement and expect the traditional laws of countervail to apply". But the omnibus trade legislation currently before the U.S. Congress contains 15 new protectionist moves by the United States which are harmful to Canada.
The Prime Minister said that the American countervail and anti-dumping laws could not apply. This new Bill applies 15 separate new measures. These new measures did not even exist when the Prime Minister signed his trade deal with the President. These measures include a redefinition of subsidy which is unfavourable to Canada, and a provision for monitoring our products which is unfavourable to Canada.
Could the Deputy Prime Minister tell us how his Minister for International Trade could say yesterday that the American Bill is, to use the Minister's words, "likely a Bill we can live with", when there are now rules in that Bill which are worse than when the Prime Minister signed his deal with the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and President of the Treasury Board):

subtopic: UNITED STATES OMNIBUS TRADE BILL-APPLICATION OF COUNTERVAIL MEASURES

Representations are certainly being made from Canadian

authorities in an attempt to modify some of the areas of concern to us.

speakeroldname: Mr. John N.Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
The
document reintroduced in the House yesterday is a discussion consensus of the two Houses of the United States Congress. Mr. Speaker, the argument made by the present Minister of International Trade that we need the trade agreement to protect us from the omnibus bill before the United States Congress is dishonest and false because this very bad U.S. law is included in the trade agreement under Section 1904. The Prime Minister therefore agreed that this bad law would be automatically included in his trade agreement. How can the Deputy Prime Minister continue to maintain, together with his minister, that Canada is sheltered from the American law and that the Prime Minister's agreement improves the situation when he knows very well that this argument is completely misleading? speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

Mr. Speaker, to the extent that there are any inconsistencies between the omnibus Trade Bill and the free trade agreement, certainly the Government of Canada will pursue those issues with vigour. It is our expectation that the United States of America will live up to the spirit of the free trade agreement, and that is what we will be working toward.
Whether or not we have an omnibus Trade Bill, there is clearly no doubt that Canadians will be much better off under a bilateral trading arrangement with the United States, as is proposed, to settle disputes by a neutral body on a binational basis, plus all the other inherent benefits that will accrue to Canadians.
I know that the Leader of the Opposition has consistently tried to discredit the agreement. I know that it is still his desire to rip it up. There are many millions of Canadians who hold a different view, and perhaps one of these days the Hon. Leader of the Opposition may have to reconsider his position.

April 15, 1988

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. On Monday, April 11, the Prime Minister said in the House that his Government was disappointed with the solution proposed by Saskatchewan to comply with the recent Supreme Court decision. Page 14325, the Government Leader in the Senate quotes on the Government's position, expressing his disappointment with this legislation and hoping that the Government of Saskatchewan would go much further in protecting minority rights. Again on Monday, the Prime Minister announced to us that three ministers were to negotiate with Saskatchewan, that they had visited Saskatchewan on the weekend. On Tuesday morning, Grant Devine said, "No way, I'm not going to change a thing." On Wednesday, the Prime Minister told me that fundamental rights are not negotiable.
What have the ministers been doing since April 8? Are they negotiating Canadians' fundamental rights with Mr. Devine or do these rights really exist today in the Constitution?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find the question a little puzzling from the Hon. Member who is normally quite up to date with respect to these important minority language rights.
If the Hon. Member wants to be correct with respect to the record, the fact is that indeed there are ongoing discussions between senior Ministers of the Saskatchewan Government, senior Ministers of the federal Government, the Prime Minister, and the Premier. This is for the very purpose of dealing with a situation which has intruded itself by virtue of a judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada. It requires leadership on the part of not only the Premier of Saskatchewan but also the federal Government.
April 15, 1988

The Prime Minister had a very full discussion with the Premier yesterday for some two hours, looking at the implications of the Mercure decision. There are areas with which we are not au courant. But the fact is that we are working together in a constructive and positive way.
I wish to point out to the Hon. Member that Premier Devine has made a very important statement with respect to the position he sees for Saskatchewan, and he is moving toward Saskatchewan becoming a part of a bilingual Canada, for which he should be given full credit. We are now trying to give the assistance of the federal Government in any way we can to move the process along so that equity for minorities across the country will in fact be recognized.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

I trust the Prime Minister will agree with me that basic and vested rights
are not negotiable.

views. There are no differences between the Hon. Member and myself.

Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries, and it has to do with the boarding yesterday by Canadian authorities of a French vessel. I wonder if the Minister could bring the House up to date as to what the Government's intentions are with respect to the event yesterday and with respect to the people who were apprehended.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to indicate to the Hon. Member that we made a statement at 10.30 this morning on this issue indicating that the vessel, the Croix de Lorraine, has been successfully apprehended after suspicion of fishing contrary to Canadian law. Mr. Speaker, could the Minister tell us what the Government has heard from the Government of France in respect of this issue? Has the Government of France officially disowned this provocative action? speechtext: do not intend to comment on the position or otherwise of the Government of France in this matter, Mr. Speaker. POSSIBLE EFFECT ON NEGOTIATIONS WITH FRANCE

Is the Government prepared to seek that kind of message from the Government of France? What effect does the Government foresee it having on negotiations between Canada and France, if France is not prepared to disown this action and

April 15, 1988

is prepared to see it as part of the way in which it hopes to succeed in its negotiations with Canada?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: CONCENTRATION OF CONTROL AND SWITCHING OF RAILWAY TRAFFIC-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. I would like to indicate to the Minister the concern of Members on this side of the House regarding CN's rationalization plan, which would concentrate control over all railway traffic in Eastern Canada in the Toronto area and in the process shift 100 jobs from Montreal to Toronto. We raised the issue earlier in March, when the oddball Minister from Newfoundland who was then Minister of Transport gave us the following answer, no more: "I was not consulted by CN on this proposal which would involve the loss of 100 jobs in Montreal".
I would like to ask the Minister of Transport whether CN management is keeping him informed of plans as sinister as the one I just described, and whether he has expressed his firm disagreement with a project that would threaten hundreds of jobs in the Montreal area.

subsubtopic: CONCENTRATION OF CONTROL AND SWITCHING OF RAILWAY TRAFFIC-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would certainly not assume CN's plans are sinister. I will wait and see exactly what is going to happen. The Hon. Member knows perfectly well, in this connection, that following an accident, the Canadian Transport Commission had advised Canadian National that it should tighten up its safety regulations. CN is now assessing a number of options, including centralizing security operations. However, I think it is premature to say that Canadian National wants to proceed with an operation of this kind and would do so at the earliest opportunity. I repeat that this is certainly not the case, although I certainly intend to keep informed and keep a close watch on developments. If a decision of this kind is taken by
CN, we intend to consider the various options with the Corporation.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect, I would like to make it clear to the Minister that we feel it is imperative that part of railway traffic control operations continue to be based in Montreal and take place in French.
I would like to ask the Minister to commit himself to opposing any plan that would export these specialized jobs, where French is spoken, from Montreal to any other part of the country.
Could the Minister at least give us a commitment that he will not approve a plan of this kind?

Mr. Speaker, by giving this kind of commitment, I would be making assumptions about decisions the Corporation has yet to make, and I would be assuming that given the proposed options, Canadian National would not consider the concerns you mentioned.
Railway security and the use of French in security services are issues we feel are very important. But once again, the Hon. Member must recognize the fact that we will have to let Canadian National look at the various options, and we will monitor developments and bear in mind the Hon. Member's concerns.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF WAR-EFFECT ON STARVING PEOPLES
CONTINUATION OF WAR-EFFECT ON STARVING PEOPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is another question which I would like the Deputy Prime Minister to explore with his colleagues. As he knows, Resolution 390 passed by the United Nations some years ago, recognized the autonomy of Eritrea and Tygre in confederation with Ethiopia. The war occurring there now is in contradiction to that resolution and underlies the starvation and deprivation occurring in that country.
Will the Government take initiatives in the United Nations to seek a solution to that war based on the contents of Resolution 390 and, in addition, in bringing this before the United Nations, to address the culpability of the Ethiopian Government in taking aid deliverers out of Ethiopia who are trying desperately to feed the Ethiopian people?

speechtext:

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF ANGOLAN VICE-MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his very important question. I am very pleased with the response that I received to my announcement on behalf of the Government. speechtext: What's his name?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
This is hard for the Leader of the Opposition. He is used to Senators criticizing his policies. I believe that such support by Senators of our policy is a very helpful and hopeful sign.
With respect to the question that was posed, I want to remind the Hon. Member that I had the honour as Government House Leader to bring in a number of reforms to the process and procedures of the House of Commons, including the scrutiny of all Governor in Council appointments. At that time in its wisdom the House decided, with the co-operation of opposition Parties in this process, to exclude judicial appointments as such. However, we have moved to consult widely. This process is an important step.
In terms of Meech Lake, we are now involved with consulting the provincial levels of government as well with respect to appointments to the Supreme Court of Canada. We are expanding accountability. It is very important in this age of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms that we have widespread input with respect to appointments made to the bench.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. The Minister's announcement yesterday about the establishment of review committees for federal judicial appointments is, in my opinion, a major step forward in the process of creating a fully open and public appointments process.

Mr. Speaker, the report of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board into the cause of the 1985 air disaster in Gander, Newfoundland, which killed 248 U.S. servicemen and eight crew members, has been sent to interested parties in Gander, Newfoundland, and in the United States. It excludes key evidence that cyanide was found in the blood of many of the 248 who were killed.
I ask the Minister of Transport this. Will he order that this report be withdrawn by the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, and order that another report be drawn up which would include all the evidence found during the autopsies that were

April 15, 1988
Oral Questions
done, including the fact that most likely many of the servicemen had breathed in deadly gas prior to the crash?

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate is normally well informed about transport matters. He knows full well that the report to which he refers is a draft report tabled in December for all parties. Those parties have requested to be heard again by the board, which is what is being done at the present time.
When an official report is issued in due course I believe the Minister will have to ask some questions or make some comments. It would be imprudent at this period of time for the Minister of Transport to comment on anything concerning what we call the draft report.

Mr. Speaker, half the members of the Aviation Safety Board disagree with the findings of the report that has been sent out. How can the Minister be satisfied with the draft report that has been sent out? Does he not agree that those people who live around airports in Canada have a right to know all the facts surrounding air disasters? If that is the way that investigations are to be carried out by the Government then perhaps we should investigate the Aviation Safety Board.

Mr. Speaker, the premise of the question bothers me somewhat. I believe that the Hon. Member would not want me to comment on a leaked report. If there is anything which has to be said about what happened in Gander it must be said in an official way. That official way will be the report that is to be tabled. I will have to see what I can do. I will consider very seriously the recommendations made by the board.
At the present time, once again, I believe it would be very imprudent to make any serious comment about what happened in Gander that day.

Mr. Speaker, my question is on the same subject to the Minister of Transport. This is my first chance to ask him a question since his appointment. I want to congratulate him on it. I wish him well. He will need all the help he can get. I will be glad to help if he will accept some of my policies.
I am assuming that the Minister has received a copy of this report, whether it is draft, preliminary, or whatever. Will he confirm whether it is true or not true that key evidence, as my hon. friend pointed out earlier, has been excluded from the report, and that other matters such as the likelihood that the aircraft was on fire, experienced a loss of power, had problems with reverse thrust of an outer starboard engine and elevator trimmer flaps, were excluded from the report as well?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for his best wishes. I would have more respect for the Hon. Member than I have for his policies.
The answer has to be the same as the one I gave to the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate. Once again, it is a draft report. The Government is one of the parties which could be heard again by the Canadian Aviation Safety Board. I think that any comment by the Minister could prejudice the quality of the report itself when it is issued by the board.
I think it would be better to await the official report, not the draft report which we received in December.

Mr. Speaker, it is absolutely essential that the Canadian Aviation Safety Board have the utmost of credibility and confidence of the public. It has been riven with internal wrangling, bickering, and other allegations. How a board could have a meeting and make a decision on a draft, or whatever kind of report, with half the board members absent looks to me as it it is not conducting its affairs properly.
Will the Minister get hold of the Aviation Safety Board, see to it that its operations are improved and straightened out, get us a new chairman who has the confidence of all concerned, and have it again go over its investigation concerning the Gander crash?

Mr. Speaker, what I said before is still true. The Canadian Aviation Safety Board has a very good record. In 1987 there were 500 reports for the Minister of Transport. They were all considered very carefully and very seriously.
I believe that the Hon. Member will agree that I never have and I will not start to comment about a leak. If we have to make any comment, it has to be done in the regular way. In the meantime, this is a serious issue. I think we all agree that this is the worst air disaster which has happened in the country. We have to give time to the board to make an official report and at the same time ensure that what will be recommended to the Minister of Transport will be the best. For that reason I think my friend will agree that we have to give some time and await what I call the official report of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board.

the interests of front-line states and against Canada. Is that the Canadian Government's policy? If it is not, why is Radio-Canada International doing that?

East): Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration, whom I congratulate on her recent appointment.

April 15, 1988

On Tuesday of this week, the Standing Committee on Labour said that special retraining and adjustment programs were necessary to deal with the U.S. trade agreement. In December, the Standing Committee on International Trade said the same thing.
In these circumstances, when will the Government announce special adjustment and retraining programs in anticipation of the U.S. trade agreement? When will the Government do something about this very important matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: EFFECTS OF CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-REQUEST FOR SPECIAL RETRAINING AND ADJUSTMENT PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his congratulations, and I appreciate them. However, I do have to correct the impression he has given to the House about what will happen after free trade.
That same report says that calculations suggest an estimated net gain of 251,000 jobs, resulting from about 439,000 being created. It says that set against the number of jobs that appear and disappear each year under the impetus of competitive realities, technological shifts, changes in consumer tastes and so on, or against the three million new jobs that will be filled during the same period as the labour force grows, these are not large numbers.
We have also made it clear that we have in place a labour adjustment board from the private sector which will help workers take advantage of new opportunities in more sophisticated industries as a result of free trade. That is good for Canadians. Those are better jobs and we are standing by Canadian workers to fill them.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, the report says that the dislocation and adjustment set in train by the trade agreement will certainly be important for the people involved. In fact, jobs will be lost in 17 manufacturing areas and the new jobs will be in service sectors, very different types of jobs.
Two committees of the House made up of a majority of Conservative members prepared unanimous reports indicating that new training and adjustment programs were necessary. Will the Minister not read those reports and listen to the Standing Committees of the House instead of rejecting them outright?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Standing Committee for its work on labour adjustment and on the Canadian Jobs Strategy. As the Hon. Member knows, we have already met many of its recommendations.
All the reports say that compared with the normal economic adjustments that are to be made, we expect minimal adjustment. Within the Canadian Jobs Strategy we have the correct mechanism to help people adjust, as we do on an ongoing basis.
I agree with the Hon. Member. Of course this is important to the people who are affected. It is very important to them. However, other job adjustment is important to people who are affected as well. Separating out the factors that go into job adjustment every year is part of our job. We do that all the time, as the Hon. Member knows, and will continue to do it under free trade, and make sure that the people affected do have an opportunity to take advantage of the new opportunities created by free trade.

subsubtopic: CRIMINAL CODE-REQUEST FOR STRENGTHENING OF PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. On November 8, 1984, the then Conservative Minister of Justice promised the House the following:
The area of hate propaganda will be dealt with and those amendments will
come after Christmas as well.
Given the serious weakness of the existing Criminal Code hate literature provisions, a weakness demonstrated most recently in the case of the virulently anti-Semitic books and articles written by Moncton teacher Malcom Ross and also demonstrated by the offensive writings of R. L. Smith in British Columbia, inciting violence against Slocan Valley environmentalists, does the Government remain committed to strengthening hate literature laws as promised over three years

ago? If so, when will the Minister finally bring forward this long overdue legislation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CRIMINAL CODE-REQUEST FOR STRENGTHENING OF PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question. I should point out that I will have an opportunity of discussing this matter with my provincial counterparts at the next meeting of federal-provincial Ministers to be held in Quebec City at the end of May.
We are looking at this particular section of the Criminal Code, and the Hon. Member will be the first one to understand that under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms one has to consider Criminal Code amendments in light of the balance which has to be demonstrated between, on the one hand, the type of statements which cause harm and damage and, on the other, the right of freedom of speech.

subsubtopic: CRIMINAL CODE-REQUEST FOR STRENGTHENING OF PROVISIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister is suggesting that he is just looking at these possibilities. He is backing away from the commitment made by his predecessor.

I am asking this Minister of Justice if he is prepared to make the same commitment made by his predecessor to amend these laws which are simply not enforceable right now? Will he take that important step?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the difficulty we often have with the NDP is that they find it very easy to get up and suggest we take all sorts of legislative action. Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Minister of Finance and it concerns the manufacturers sales tax which the Minister of Finance describes as a silent killer of jobs even though he goes on using it more and more. As the Canadian Chamber of Commerce pointed out, the last Budget increase in the rate of sales tax creates a bias in that Canadian produced capital goods will attract a tax of up to 14 per cent, while imports are taxed 2 1/2 per cent less.

they see it, Canadian sovereignty is threatened by the proposed trade deal between the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) and the President of the U.S., which the Prime Minister had absolutely no mandate to negotiate given his approach to the people in the last election. subsubtopic: PROHIBITION OF DISCRIMINATION ON GROUNDS OF SEXUAL ORIENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in February, 1985, the Government ordered the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs to prepare a report on equality rights in Canada. In March of 1986 the Government accepted this report and its recommendation, saying it would take whatever measures necessary to ensure that sexual orientation is a prohibited ground of discrimination. As the Government has yet to introduce significant legislation acting upon these recommendations supported by the Government, the petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to ensure that the Government and Parliament act to implement all the recommendations contained in this report as specified above with all due haste and speed.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPARATIONS TO VICTIMS OF EXPERIMENTS AT ALLAN MEMORIAL INSTITUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition signed by a number of residents of Oshawa and Toronto, Ontario; from Edmonton; and from various other cities in Canada who note that the Canadian Government funded unethical brainwashing experiments of the late psychiatrist, D. Ewen Cameron, which were conducted at the Allan Memorial Institute in Montreal in the 1950s and early 1960s.
They note that many Canadians were permanently damaged, both psychologically and neurologically, by these experiments which were inflicted on them without their knowledge or consent. A number of these individuals are suing the CIA in the United States for its complicity. They note, finally, that the Canadian Government has refused to admit its legal or moral responsibility for these Canadians or to offer them any reparations for their permanent damage, pain, and suffering.
They therefore call upon Parliament to release all incriminating evidence to assist them, to acknowledge the legal and moral responsibility of the Government of Canada to these Canadians, and to offer reparations to these Canadians who were victims of such unethical experiments.
April 15, 1988

subsubtopic: PROHIBITION OF DISCRIMINATION ON GROUNDS OF SEXUAL ORIENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have another petition which is signed primarily by residents of Ontario, mais, il y a aussi beaucoup de residants de Montreal et de la Ville de Quebec. These petitioners note that over two years ago the Government of Canada accepted the unanimous report of the Subcommittee on Equality Rights and its recommendations and said that it would take whatever measures were necessary to ensure that sexual orientation is a prohibited ground of discrimination.
They note that the Government has not yet acted on this important promise and therefore urge the Government to implement the recommendations contained in that report with all due haste and speed.

Mr. Speaker, I have another petition signed by a large number of residents of Burnaby, my own constituency, who express their deep concern about the implications of the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal for Canada.
They note that the Government had no mandate from the Canadian people to negotiate this trade deal. In fact, they note that during the course of these negotiations the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised that Canadian sovereignty would not be compromised. They note that this deal would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine our own economic future and undermine our ability to build a society distinct from that of the United States.
They therefore call upon the Government to dissolve Parliament and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject this profoundly dangerous agreement during a national general election.
