speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (for the Minister of the Environment) moved
speechtext: that Bill C-30, an Act to amend the National Parks Act and to amend an Act to amend the National Parks Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to see Bill C-30, an Act to amend the National Parks Act, brought forward for second reading. Bill C-30 represents the first major overhaul of this Act since it was proclaimed more than half a century ago. The 37 proposed amendments are a measure of the Government's commitment to national parks and of the extent to which the current Act is outdated. The amendments proposed in the House of Commons will provide this country with an integrated, contemporary and forward-looking conservation framework for our national parks.
Reform is long overdue. For example, when the first poaching provisions for national parks were set in 1919, a $500 maximum fine may have been sufficiently onerous to deter violators. Now, however, that fine really represents a licence to kill.

April 15, 1988
National Parks Act
Modern poachers of park wildlife are part of a highly organized, lucrative, international criminal network. The stakes are very high. A trophy head of Dali's sheep can command $50,000, a live falcon $20,000. Taking rare and endangered species anywhere on this planet is indeed a crime, not just against the animal or that species, but a crime against humanity. The taking of such animals from within the boundaries of wilderness areas protected by our most stringent conservation law is an outrage.
Meaningful sanctions must be put in place and enforced. The amendments before us today will create maximum penalties of $150,000 or six months in jail. These penalties will be matched by a tough new enforcement regime, with the help of the RCMP.
For poachers of non-threatened species for meat or fur, the Bill proposes a fine of $2,000. However, we have concluded that that will not be enough. Therefore, the Government will seek an additional amendment to increase fines to $10,000 or six months in jail.
Let me highlight some of the main provisions of Bill C-30. Fines will be increased for destructive activities in our parks, such as use of all terrain vehicles in ecologically sensitive areas. A new provision will allow for traditional subsistence activities in new parks, such as hunting and fishing, by native communities. An enabling section will allow self- government for the towns of Jasper and Banff if and when and residents so elect. The Bill will also allow the setting of legislative boundaries for the two towns, will limit the development of new commercial ski areas, and restrict any further transportation and energy supply corridors through our parks.
Provisions will also be made for a citizens' heritage fund to allow Canadians to contribute directly to our national parks system. Amendments will regulate the use of pesticides in parks.
The Bill provides for the establishment of Ellesmere Island National Park in the far North and Grasslands National Park, which we hope will soon be a reality in Saskatchewan.
The Government will also ask the legislative committee to propose the necessary amendments to create our first national marine park, combined with the terrestrial park at Bruce Peninsula in the great Province of Ontario.
I want to go into some detail on the poaching provisions of the amendment. Under the proposed amendments, poaching on certain species of endangered and trophy animals indeed would be subject to a maximum fine of $150,000 on summary conviction, or in the case of a conviction and indictment, a maximum fine of $150,000 or up to six months in prison, or both.
Poaching of all other wildlife would be subject to a maximum fine of $2,000 on summary conviction. The inadequacy of the penalties for poaching in national parks has been cited repeatedly by judges annoyed by the reliance on multiple
charges and forfeiture of vehicles and equipment to create at least some deterrent to poaching.
The current maximum fine of $500 has been in effect since 1919 and is inadequate as a deterrent to poaching.
Combatting organized poaching activities is of particular concern. Provisions to proceed by indictment should serve as a deterrent both to the organizers and their clients who are often wealthy individuals.
How serious is this problem of poaching in national parks? Since many poaching incidents go undetected, it is difficult to provide accurate statistics on the problem. However, in the mountain parks it is estimated that at least 50 animals are poached each year, many of which are trophy animals.
The poaching of trophy animals is not a problem of large numbers being taken but rather the significance of losing any of these animals. Not only is the public deprived of the opportunity to view them in the wild, the loss of even a few prime animals each year can affect the long-term health of their populations.
These animals are still relatively abundant in the national parks, and as they become scarce in areas where they can be hunted legally, the parks are becoming more and more attractive to poachers. Perhaps the most insidious aspect of the problem has been the development of the sophisticated organized poaching rings.
In parks where animals are poached primarily for meat, the incidents of poaching are much higher. Estimates of up to 100 or 200 incidents of poaching a year are not uncommon in some parks.
The actual number of incidents of poaching vary from park to park, depending on local factors such as access to game close to park boundaries and along highway corridors, park size, and the actual types of species within the park. Recent studies in several U.S. states show that only about 5 per cent of poaching incidents are ever detected.
Based on a more conservative estimate that 20 per cent of poaching incidents are detected, it is suspected that about 50 big game animals are poached in the mountain parks each year. This would include many that are on the schedule that is available to those persons interested.
On the same basis, it is estimated that on average a total of 800 big game animals are poached each year in all national parks.
Poaching of trophy animals is particularly of concern in mountain parks and Kluane National Park in the Yukon Territory.
Poaching in the parks is very serious and is very much a part of the amendments we are discussing today. Wildlife that is not covered under Section 8(1.1) are poached primarily for their meat. The $2,000 maximum fine exceeds the highest prices paid for big game carcasses in the black market for
April 15, 1988

wildlife meat. This fine is in the mid-range of similar penalties in the provinces and territories.
Across the country, the array of penalties for poaching is complex. Penalties vary depending on several factors, such as the species involved, the poaching methods used, and whether or not the case involved is the first or second offence.
Some jurisdictions include provisions for imprisonment. On balance, the $2,000 maximum fine is already falling below comparable penalties in the provinces and territories, and several jurisdictions have recently increased their levels. Therefore, the Government will propose an additional amendment to increase fines to $10,000 or six months in jail on indictment, which would put the penalty back in the top range. Another species schedule relating to wildlife which are poached primarily for meat or fur would trigger this penalty.
We are very pleased that in relation to penalties for poaching in national parks, a special budget has been established to fund the activities of warden enforcement support teams. These teams will be deployed to parks where poaching is a problem in order to boost enforcement capabilities at key times of the year. A number of special surveillance operations have been initiated this year to coincide with the fall season. Park officials are in the process of renewing their law enforcement procedures and training programs to identify areas where improvements will be made.
The feasibility of an awards program for information leading to the conviction of poachers is under investigation also. An agreement with the RCMP for greater co-operation in law enforcement in national parks has been drafted and signed. That part of the amendment is very important.
I would just like to refer to another section of the Act, which is the traditional subsistence activities. There are two groups implicated by these provisions, the traditional subsistence use by local people, and the traditional subsistence use by native groups. The former are, in some cases, dependent on resources in a park area for their subsistence needs. The latter have both subsistence and cultural associations with the land and its resources. These activities are generally fishing, trapping, woodcutting and other limited use of renewable resources.
Subsistence resource use has been an issue since the early 1970s, both in public consultations and in federal-provincial negotiations. The rights of native people to hunt and fish for domestic purposes must be respected and integrated into park planning and management in the context of claims and establishment negotiations. Similarly, concessions have been made to certain resource uses by non-native local people in order to avoid detrimental impact on the livelihood of such residents. Non-native resource uses would only apply for one or more generations where no alternatives exist outside the park.
National Parks Act
Controls will allow natives or local users to continue to exercise their traditional practices while allowing parks to fulfil their mandate to protect natural heritage resources. All such activities are subject to the requirement to protect natural resources of the park. Providing the continuation of subsistence level activities will permit the creation of new parks for the benefit of all Canadians while at the same time not penalizing local people who have traditionally relied on the area for the necessities of life.
For natives, such activities as hunting and fishing have been an essential part of their culture for thousands of years. Such subsistence activities would be closely monitored and regulated where necessary to ensure the maintenance of viable populations of fish and wildlife.
The amendment is intended to provide a greater degree of protection for the wilderness areas of national parks. Over the last few years, conservation groups and northern native groups have expressed concern that wilderness areas could in the future be subjected to increased pressure for development of visitor facilities, and they should, therefore, be given added protection in the law. This amendment will ensure that wilderness areas remain essentially undeveloped lands and that any proposed change to the boundaries of a wilderness area will be open for public review, not only during the park planning process but also through the regulatory process.
As new national park plans are completed, or existing park plan management plans are reviewed with the public, it is the Government's intention to recommend designation of its wilderness areas to the Governor in Council.
I would like to go to another section of this Act which concerns pollution. We have recently passed the Environmental Protection Act. We are very pleased it has passed committee stage and has come back into the House for third reading. It deals with toxic chemicals. I would like to mention here pollution in national parks as related to these amendments. Section 8(1.3) reads:
... recognizes the special status of national park lands as areas set aside for the benefit of all Canadians. Its effect, and that of (1.4), (1.5), and (1.6) which follow it, is to provide the necessary level of protection to the environment and ensure public health and safety in parks. These amendments will limit the deleterious effects of potentially harmful substances by giving the Minister the ability to take action forthwith if compliance does not occur, and to recover costs for any such mitigating activities. It is important to note that existing and proposed legislation can be used where an incident is of such great proportions that a much higher penalty is called for.
Modern society produces or uses many substances that can adversely affect natural processes or threaten human health. Parks are not exempt from these consequences of industrialization. Recognizing that this danger exists, it is imperative to minimize any negative impact as quickly and effectively as possible. When the person discharging or depositing an undesirable substance will not take responsibility, significant measures would be allowed both to force action and to exact payment when Her Majesty must undertake the appropriate action.

April 15, 1988
National Parks Act
You may recall, Mr. Speaker, that on May 14 of last year, this House made history by unanimously endorsing a resolution for the protection of the South Moresby area of the Queen Charlotte Islands of British Columbia as a national park reserve. In the last three and a half years, more new parks have been created than in the previous decade and a half. Indeed none were established in that desolate period. This Government is a parks Government. We intend not only to save individual wilderness areas as parks but to lay the groundwork for the completion of our national parks' system.
Over 100 years ago Sir John A. Macdonald established Canada's first national park in what is now Banff. Since then Canada's parks system has become the best in the world encompassing over 140,000 square kilometres and attracting some 25 million visitors every year. We are proud of that as Canadians.
The environmental commitment made by Sir John A. Macdonald to protect and preserve Canada's unique natural beauty is being continued by this Government. In addition to creating three new parks and introducing these amendments, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) commissioned a national task force on new park establishment chaired by Professor John Theberge of the University of Waterloo. The mandate of the commission was to propose new ideas for expanding our national parks system.
One of the key recommendations of the task force was to urge all levels of government to work together and to develop new ways of preserving unique natural areas. A new designation called Heritage Lands was also proposed by the task force. It could act as a mechanism for protecting more unique wilderness areas. An example of how this designation could be used can be found in the City of Scarborough, that part of Canada that 1 have the honour and privilege of representing.
The Rouge River Valley which winds its way through 5,000 acres of wilderness in northeast Scarborough represents the last wildlife area in Metropolitan Toronto. The valley is home to white-tailed deer, coyotes, red fox, and a host of nationally rare birds and plant life. The valley also serves as a huge outdoor classroom for thousands of school children who visit the area to learn about nature and conservation.
Unfortunately, the Ontario Government, which owns virtually all of the land, is considering using this precious natural area for luxury housing, or indeed it even talked about a garbage dump. The people of Scarborough and the people of Canada cannot let that happen. Once we lose an area like the Rouge, we can never get it back.
Earlier this week I invited representatives of Save the Rouge Valley Citizens' Group in Scarborough to come to Ottawa and bring this important issue to the attention of Members of Parliament. I was especially honoured that you, Mr. Speaker, took the time to meet with the group and you expressed your support for saving the Rouge Valley.
Mir. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton): Save the Rouge.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext: Members of Parliament are saying that saving the Rouge is very important to the House of Commons.
It is extremely important to Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Also this week the federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) joined me in a tour of the Rouge. He offered his support for preserving the valley. In fact, the federal Government has provided nearly $80,000 to date to the Save the Rouge Valley organization to help them direct public attention to this issue and persuade the Province of Ontario to listen to the people.
The recommendations of this task force report, together with the outstanding parks record of the Minister of the Environment, should be enough to convince the Ontario Government to work with Environment Canada to protect this environmentally significant area.
In conclusion, when the House stood together to save South Moresby, we accomplished a dream. We now have an opportunity to realize another dream in Scarborough, and in all the special wildlife areas across Canada.
As Wildlife Week draws to a close, it is appropriate that we are discussing Bill C-30. It is only fitting that we give speedy passage to Bill C-30, because, as the task force noted, national parks do not impede our future, they anchor it.

Mr. Speaker, to the Parliamentary Secretary and to her Minister I would like to say that this day could well be described as a red letter day for Canada's national parks. It is a red letter day that has taken a little while to get here. By my calculations, it has been 487 days since the Bill was first introduced. However, we now have the Bill, and we want to see it move quickly through all stages and become the law of the land.
The amendments to the National Parks Act which are contained in Bill C-30 are amendments that we in the Liberal Party, the Official Opposition, in principle welcome. It should be noted that these amendments have not come about suddenly. They were developed through a long process of evolution that goes back for quite a number of years in the recent history of our country.
It was in the 1970s that there began some extensive national public consultations regarding a new parks policy. These consultations led to the 1978 statement on a new national parks policy. The House ought to know that most of the amendments that are found in Bill C-30 that we are debating today were actually introduced into Cabinet and approved in the Liberal administration in the month of March, 1984. They did not reach the House in the form of a Bill prior to the dissolution of that Parliament.
The Bill that we are dealing with today, Bill C-30, could really be called Liberal legislation. But even putting that aside,
April 15, 1988

we could certainly describe it as liberal in spirit. The amendments find support on this side of the House.
I want to point out again that it did take a long while for these amendments to be debated at second reading stage. In fact, it took the Government two full years from when it first took office to even recognize that national parks were needed. I say that because there was no mention of national parks in the Government's program until the Throne Speech of October, 1986. In the Throne Speech it states:
Canada's National Parks represent a heritage of great importance to the
present and future generations. My government will ask Parliament to approve
major reforms to the National Parks Act...
That can be found at page 12 of Hansard on October 1, 1986.
Shortly thereafter, in the same month, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) told the House:
The Parks amendments will be ready for first reading in Parliament soon,
and I urge the Opposition to give them expeditious passage.
That can be found at page 290 of Hansard on October 10, 1986.
Finally, on December 11, 1986 the Minister tabled Bill C-30 for first reading and now it is back in the House for the first time for expeditious passage.
Ever since Bill C-30 was given that first reading in 1986 we in this Party, parks and conservation groups, and the general public have been asking the Government when the second reading debate is going to take place. They have asked: "Why is second reading debate being postponed for such a long period of time? Why is the Minister's desire for expeditious passage being frustrated?"
I think we have a few clues about why there has been such a long delay in what I am describing as a red letter day for Canada's national parks. We know, for example, that in Banff National Park the operators of the Sunshine Village ski area want to expand their boundaries and move into some ecologically sensitive areas, those that are known as the Sunshine Meadows. With the passage of Bill C-30 they will not be able to do that. One of the most important aspects of Bill C-30 is that it clearly sets out the boundaries of ski areas in three parks-Banff, Jasper, and Riding Mountain. If one were interested, one could look at the Bill and find the boundaries in Schedule III on page 41 of the Bill. Incidentally, those were the same boundaries that were agreed to in 1978.
It is this boundary question for developers which has made the Bill controversial, not among the Parties in the House but within the ranks of the governing Party itself. The so-called developers have some very strong allies. They certainly have behind them the Government of Alberta, and they have certainly had with them many, if not all, Alberta Conservative caucus federal Members of Parliament. These two powerful groups-the Alberta caucus of the Government and the
National Parks Act
Alberta Government-have applied some enormous pressure on the Minister of the Environment regarding the boundaries contained in Bill C-30.
I believe and I hope that the fact we are now debating Bill C-30 at second reading today is testimony to the fact that the Minister of the Environment has withstood those pressures. It still has to go to the legislative committee and come back to the House at report stage. However, if the Bill survives without major amendments, particularly to the section dealing with the boundaries for development, I will credit the Minister with having scored a very major victory in the name of parks.
I want to return to the kind of opposition the Minister of the Environment has had to face. On December 15, 1987, The Edmonton Journal featured an article entitled "Parks plan 'held hostage' by Alta. MPs". The writer of this piece, Mr. Ed Struzik of the Ottawa Bureau of The Edmonton Journal, wrote as follows:
The future of Canada's national parks is being "held hostage" by the Alberta Conservative caucus, say federal officials and national environment leaders.
At issue are persistent attempts by the caucus to change Bill C-30, a National Parks Act amendment.
The MPs want to allow more tourism and resource development, taking a stand that's almost a carbon copy of a confidential Alberta government paper presented to Environment Minister Tom McMillan.
In referring to that Alberta government paper, the article indicates:
It calls for expansion of ski hills and townsites in the mountain parks.
The matter has become so critical that McMillan, who rejects the Alberta position, is considering calling in the country's conservation leaders to gather support for the Bill, sources say.
The Minister said last week that "if we suburbanize national parks, we'll kill them".
A senior Environment official confirmed McMillan is becoming frustrated by the "stubbornness" of the Alberta MPs.
"They are a powerful force and if they continue, they could kill the bill altogether," the official said.
The power of ignorance.

I thank my Hon. friend for his useful contribution to the debate with that interjection.
The article continues:
John Theberge, chairman of a ministerial task force on national parks, said if Alberta had its way it will mean the end of the national park system in Canada.
"It seems that a lot of people, particularly the Alberta caucus and the Alberta government, have lost sight of the fact that parks were not established to promote tourism opportunities."
The bill was introduced in Parliament a year ago and still hasn't received second reading.
The article is dated December 15, 1987 and goes on to indicate:
Keven MacNamee, executive director of the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society, said: "What really bothers me is that cabinet has

approved these amendments. This Bill could die and it will be completely the fault of the Alberta caucus."
Alberta has "no right holding the rest of the country hostage" because of its "greedy desire" for more economic opportunities, he said.
If the bill dies, he said new national parks like Gros Morne, Northern Ellesmere, Bruce Peninsula and South Moresby may never be given full park status because of legal obstacles only the proposed amendments can clear.
I have taken a little time to read from the article to set the debate in some kind of context because it is a major piece of legislation. What we are doing today is extremely important for the future of our parks.
I suppose it is never fair when one deals with an article not to allow the other side to give its point of view. The same article tells us the position of the chairman of the Alberta caucus of the federal Government. He said that the Bill currently before us "is good, but it's just too airtight". The Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) went on to say:
It won't allow for the enhancement of the tourism industry.
The article continues:
-he sees room for some "limited to moderate lumber developments" in national parks and the possibility of angle-drilling for oil and gas from outside the park boundaries".
Wilderness and development can go hand-in-hand in the big national parks, he said.
Although apparently this is the position of the Alberta caucus on the government side, and it is the position of the Alberta Government in a paper which it has given to the Minister, happily it is not the position taken by the people of the Province of Alberta. Some polls have been taken and reported upon, testing the views of the people of Alberta regarding national parks. They show that most Albertans support Bill C-30 and feel that the four mountain parks should be protected against further development.
I am sure that it will surprise you, Mr. Speaker, that the Alberta Government and the Alberta caucus on the government side could be out of touch with the people of Alberta. I found that to be astounding. I thought that there was great sensitivity within the Alberta caucus on the government side and in the Alberta Government on issues of this kind.
The Edmonton Journal certainly seems to be a great supporter of parks. In an April 7, 1987 editorial it took the Government of Alberta to task and asked the following question:
Will the Alberta Government ever learn that the natural resources found in Banff, Jasper, and Waterton Lakes are too important to sacrifice for the sake of convenience?
The Economic Development Minister wants Jasper National Park to become a provincial park. The Tourism Minister told an Alberta Tory convention that he strongly supports a proposal to build a six-storey hotel at the Sunshine Village ski development at Banff National Park.
The editorial concludes:
For the sake of convenience and money, they would jeopardize priceless natural resources to build condominiums on the shores of pristine mountain lakes or huge hotels on the side of a mountain.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: That is absolute nonsense.

It is. My friend says to do that would be absolute nonsense. I agree with him. The editorial agrees with the Hon. Member as well.
The editorial concludes in this way:
Tourism certainly offers great potential to diversify the province's economy. But there must be a balance between development and preservation of national parks for future generations.
I want it to be understood that the Liberal Party is committed to the passage of Bill C-30. We want those Sunshine Village boundaries to be intact. We will strongly resist and oppose any move that may be taken in the legislative committee or by the Government at report stage or whenever, either to have those boundaries removed or to have any future changes left in the hands of the Governor in Council. On this side of the House we believe that the Governor in Council would be less able to withstand the strengths of powerful lobbyists to adjust those boundaries than if we had those boundaries established in law and approved by Parliament.
The House and the country ought to know that national parks are revenue generating. They provide more than 34,000 person years of employment and over $145 million in taxes, duties and royalties for local, provincial and federal governments. That is a 300 per cent return on investment, according to the National Parks Task Force of 1986. Additionally, there is evidence that limiting development in parks is the key factor to stimulating growth in surrounding communities, in the case of Alberta such communities as Canmore and Pincher Creek, and Golden, B.C.
I have said repeatedly that we support Bill C-30, but there is in the Bill one clause that does give us some concern. It is not necessarily that we would seek to have that clause removed, but it does give us a little bit of concern. It is the clause that deals with the citizens heritage fund.
At the moment we are not in a clause-by-clause study of the Bill so I will stay away from excessive detail and deal only with the principle in this particular clause. The so-called citizens heritage fund has raised a number of questions. The Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society, for example, has written to the Minister asking some pointed questions about this fund. I will refer to just two paragraphs of the letter to the Minister which state:
During the past months, the Society has consulted with many individuals on Bill C-30. While reaction has been favourable, many expressed concern over the Citizens Heritage Fund. The proposed Fund raises three main questions: (1) Why is it being established? (2) Will it compete with existing voluntary organizations? (3) How will the Fund operate? The total lack of information on this major proposal has prompted this concern.
The letter goes on to state:
We believe the concerns expressed about the Fund are justified. A government administered Fund aimed at raising private monies to supplement

April 15, 1988

a tax based program is a fundamental shift in how government will fund the national parks program. While the Society supports in principle private initiatives to further the national parks program, clearly such involvement must evolve in an informed manner.
That is the difficulty with the citizens heritage fund. It is not evolving in an informed manner. For example, it is my understanding that this fund is to be dispensed at the discretion of the Minister. Whoever is the Minister of the Environment in charge of Parks Canada will be able to use this fund presumably as he sees fit. 1 am worried about that because it has at least the potential of being just another one of those infamous slush funds that governments like to have available. They like to have them available because at the appropriate moment in time, that is, the closer to an election it is, the more useful these funds become. They can be doled out on a regional basis with a political connotation.
We do not want that at all. After all, Parliament has been reformed. Government is being reformed. We want to be a part of that new wave. I believe that I probably have the support of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party and probably have at least a modest degree of support from the government benches in this regard.
Before winding down my contribution to this debate I want to talk about a couple of the other aspects of the Bill that I consider to be important. The Parliamentary Secretary made reference to the traditional subsistence activities that are contained in the Bill. This particular aspect of the Bill recognizes that new national parks must not inhibit traditional activities that are carried on by local people. The range of activities is broad. It goes from hunting, fishing and trapping by aboriginal peoples, to rabbit hunting and domestic wood cutting in the Atlantic region. It must be made clear that this provision does not apply retroactively to existing parks such as Banff and Jasper but that it will allow the settlement of aboriginal land claims outstanding in national park reserves, such as, for example, the claim of the Haida to South Moresby.
When a new national park was established quite a number of years ago in the constituency which I represent, the Government of Canada entered into extensive negotiations with the Robinson- Superior Treaty as to the extinguishment of their rights. These negotiations were very protracted in nature. The desire of the Government was to find an accommodation. It believed at the time that the best accommodation was to have these aboriginal rights relinquished in return for a cash compensation.
After a long period of discussion, it soon became apparent that we really cannot put a dollar value on aboriginal rights. The Government of the day had enough wisdom to drop the negotiations and say to the Robinson-Superior Treaty with reference to Pukaskwa National Park that they may retain their rights of hunting, fishing and trapping.
National Parks Act
Happily, I can report to the House that since the Government of the day made that decision, there have been no serious problems in Pukaskwa National Park. There have been no abuses by the aboriginal people. In fact, it has been proven, as I have said on other occasions, that the aboriginal people are among this nation's finest conservationists.
I would also point out that Bill C-30 provides for wilderness zones and the activities allowed therein. This gives legislative authority to a policy that is already in practice. Environment and conservation groups were hoping for something stronger, but nevertheless, these wilderness zones are now in the Bill. The policy that is in effect has been made law, and that is a welcome development.
As well, something ought to be said about the powers of expropriation. This has been described as a particular fingerprint of this particular Minister and Government. The previous Government had wanted the powers of expropriation to remain in the National Parks Act. This legislation takes away those expropriation powers. In so doing, I believe that the future negotiating position of the Government of Canada in the establishment of new national parks is weakened.
I recognize that in the past, the power of expropriation has created serious difficulties, and perhaps in some instances it could even be described as having been abused. There ought legitimately among Members of Parliament to be concern about expropriation powers. However, I would want to point out that when dealing with national parks, it is very difficult to say that there exists something that could be described as federal greed. That is hardly the case because national parks and national park reserves total only 1.5 per cent of the Canadian landscape. Who among us would say that that is too much?
The Parliamentary Secretary spent a good part of her time dealing with the question of poaching. I am pleased that she did, and there is no need for me to go over all of that ground again, except to say that it is correct and right, in our view, that poaching will now carry significantly heavier fines under the new legislation. This, I believe, well reflects the priority the public is giving today to wildlife protection. There are to be fines of up to $150,000 for poaching any one of the nine endangered species: bighorn sheep, Dali's sheep, grizzly bear, gyrfalcon, mountain goat, peregrine falcon, piping plover, polar bear and whooping crane.
I believe Hon. Members ought to know, however, that the poaching of other game animals such as caribou, elk and deer in national parks carries a much lower fine, a fine of only $2,000. We in the Official Opposition think that the poaching of game animals should carry a higher penalty. We urge the Minister to reassess that particular aspect of the poaching provisions in the Bill.
I am convinced that Canada has far too little in the way of lands that fall under the aegis of national parks. It is certainly not my view that all wilderness in Canada should be protected,

April 15, 1988
National Parks Act
but there are special places that ought to be protected like South Moresby, Jasper, Banff and other national parks.
If Bill C-30 passes unaltered, if it is not radically adjusted along the way, then I think it will strike a very positive note for the protection of what others in Canada, on many occasions, have described as a priceless national heritage, the national parks of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I was wondering when the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) would rise on a point of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have had a brief conversation with the critic for the Official Opposition who informed me that it was his understanding that there would be one speaker per Party and then we might be able to dispose of the Bill. I have not had a chance to talk to a representative of the New Democratic Party since there was some confusion today about to whom to speak. I wonder if the Members of the New Democratic Party have the same understanding or not.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) is the designated speaker today, so I imagine he would be the one who could answer.

Mr. Speaker, I am not aware of any discussions. I am aware that this Bill was sprung on us without any notice this afternoon and that the environment critic for the NDP is not present. I can only assume that she and perhaps others would want to speak on this Bill. I am afraid that I could not agree to any such proposition, given the circumstances under which the Bill was introduced.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I then recognize the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill on debate.
Your environment critic supports the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) says that the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) supports the Bill. Of course she supports it. We support the Bill. That is not the question. The question is, is this any way to run a Parliament.
At 12.30 in the afternoon on a Friday, the Government decides it will call a Bill without any notice. The environment critics for the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party are not able to be here to comment. Fortunately for both the Liberal Party and for the NDP, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) and I happened to be around.
I was around 15 months ago when this Bill was introduced. In fact, I was the NDP environment critic at that time. It was only because I was the critic at that time and because I happened to be here this afternoon that we are able to comment on this Bill in a prepared way.
There is no way that this can be considered fair play by the Government. The Government sat on this Bill for 15 months and then on a Friday afternoon in April, without any warning, it brings it forward and hopes that it can slip it into committee. It is not our intention to delay this Bill at all, but it certainly is our intention to make some comments on the principles of the Bill at second reading stage, and that is just what I intend to do and what I expect other NDP Members to be able to do as well.
I began by saying that we support the Bill. We would have liked to have seen it go through a long time ago, but because the Government itself has delayed it for 15 months, there is no reason for us now to be pressured into dealing with it in an hour and a half.
I want to take this opportunity to go over some of the shortcomings of the Bill. First, why do we support it? We support it because it does provide the legislative housekeeping needed for the smooth operation of national parks. It puts into legislation current parks policies, particularly in the limitation of future resort development in the parks system. It provides stiff fines for poaching of rare game and birds, and, as has already been mentioned, many of the parks and wilderness associations are eager to see this Bill pass. Indeed, they are eager to see it go to committee, and that is why it will go to committee after an appropriate time has been allowed for debate at second reading stage.
If this Bill was introduced 15 months ago, one might ask what has taken it so long. With all due respect to you and your province of origin, Mr. Speaker, the cause of the delay has been what we in this House sometimes call the goon squad from Alberta. This goon squad regularly stands in the way of any kind of progressive legislation the Government might be considering. It is rare enough that the Government considers progressive legislation, but when it does you always have the goon squad from Alberta trying to retard the process.
The only national park, I suppose, that would be appropriate for Alberta as far as those people are concerned would be some kind of human dinosaur park where the goon squad from Alberta could be stuffed and mounted so people could see just what political dinosaurs look like.
The NDP in Manitoba will be in a museum after the next election.
The Alberta caucus might go for that if you could convince them there was a buck to be made. That is the way they see the world. It is just a place out there waiting for a buck to be made.

We could put Howard Pawley in a museum.
April 15, 1988

The goon squad has the most morally primitive view of the world you could imagine. Any Bill that would suggest there should be areas of the planet that are left alone, where no money is made out of them, is a travesty for them of Progressive Conservative doctrine. That is the reason for the delay, the goon squad from Alberta. Enough about them; history will deal with them appropriately.
Some of the points we would like to raise and elaborate upon have to do with the requirement for the Government to be more frank with Parliament in this Bill and this debate about its intentions for various parks, particularly those which have been the object of some controversy. We need to see proposed boundaries for Banff and Jasper. We need to see any agreement with the Alberta Government that might have been arrived at prior to the Bill finally being brought forward for second reading. We need to see actual proposals for what would constitute a wilderness area, and planned use, and the details of the administration of the citizens heritage fund. These are all things we are debating in the dark because the Government refuses to give us any details.
We need to know that the Government is willing to support parks as natural preserves and not as tourist sites. We need to know that the Government is willing to allocate resources to park development without having to develop quasi-private fund-raising programs like the citizens heritage fund. What is the Government's commitment to these kinds of parks separate and apart from these private fund-raising schemes it has in mind?
In short, we need to know whether the Government has a clear and unequivocal commitment to national parks. We need to know whether there will be amendments to the Park Act which give clearly articulated principles by which the parks will be administered. Parks have suffered from too much ad hoc and discretionary decision-making already.
We need to know about amendments to the Park Act which will legislate current policy against resource development. It is not enough just to have a policy. We want to see that policy enshrined in legislation. We remember that it is not so long ago that a former unlamented Minister of the Environment, 1 cannot remember the name of her riding, spoke about logging and mining in national parks. We need legislation which prevents any Minister from suddenly getting a whim about logging and mining in national parks and permitting that sort of atrocity to go on.
What does Bill C-30 do? It expands the National Parks system. We all should regard that positively. It entrenches in legislation the establishment of Ellesmere Island National Park and provides for the future establishment of Grasslands National Park in Saskatchewan. I got some mail on that park the other day. It has been dragging on and on. Some agreement was reached with respect to I believe water rights but other negotiations are still going on.
When we think about areas that need to be preserved we quite rightly think about South Moresby or places which, by
National Parks Act
their nature, command the attention of the media and others in such a way that a grasslands national park does not. However, there is very little natural grassland left in western Canada and that in and of itself is a feature of what naturally occurs and what there was a great deal of in Canada at one point. Just as much effort should go into preserving natural prairie habitat as goes into preserving natural habitat in British Columbia, Ontario or the Atlantic provinces. I make the plea on behalf of the Grasslands National Park that it might be completed very soon.
We wonder why the Bill makes no mention of the establishment of national marine parks. The federal Cabinet approved a national marine parks policy in September, 1986, well before Bill C-30 was introduced. At the moment there are no marine parks in Canada, although there are proposals for five potential parks. One of the reasons no such park exists is that the Government has no statutory authority to establish marine parks. In its marine park policy the Government decided to create this authority with an amendment to the National Parks Act. What do we have here? Amendments to the National Parks Act but nothing with respect to marine parks, the very kind of amendments that the Government said it ought to bring in before this Bill was drafted. Perhaps there will be some explanation for the absence of those kinds of amendments.
Bill C-30 also works to eliminate poaching. Under the 1930 Parks Act the maximum fine for any transgression against a park is a $500 fine. That $500 is certainly not what it used to be, certainly not what it was in 1930. The penalty is too paltry to dissuade poachers from taking the valuable game which can be found in the parks. The Parliamentary Secretary went on at some length about that.
The Bill lists nine species deserving of protection in particular, including bighorn sheep, Dali's sheep, grizzly bear, gyrfalcon, mountain goat, peregrine falcon, piping plover, polar bear and whooping crane. It creates a penalty for poaching those animals of a maximum of $150,000 or six months in jail. It also raises to $2,000 the maximum fine for other offences under the Act. We are delighted to see that and we await the day when those kinds of penalties will be available to the Government. However, the one thing it could have done, and this is very timely given the program on The Journal a couple of weeks ago about the poaching not of these rare animals-
The Silent Slaughter.
Yes, that is what it was called, about the poaching not of animals considered to be rare but animals that are normally hunted.
Like elk.

Yes, like elk, moose or bear. The Government has not moved on that in this Bill and I hope it will. It will have an opportunity in committee to move amendments to

April 15, 1988
National Parks Act
provide stiffer penalties for the poaching of animals like black bear, moose, elk, caribou and others. Strange as it may seem, there is an incredible black market for various animal parts. I will not go into the details, Mr. Speaker, for fear of offending your great sensitivity and innocence in these things. Bear gall bladder is an example of one part for which there is great demand in Asia. With all due respect to Asian aspirations to greater virility, the people in Asia who need these products and the people who are providing them with these products should stay out of Canada, leave our wildlife alone, and sort out their assorted problems in some other way.
I hope that we will see amendments to this Act which take into account that which we have come to know since this Bill was introduced about the silent slaughter of many ordinary game animals here in Canada because once they are gone, there is no way of getting them back.
I would like to say a word about the National Parks citizens' heritage fund. The Government wishes to establish a fund to which Canadians could make tax deductible donations to expand or enhance the parks site system. Since this fund was first discussed Canadians have been trying to find out exactly what the Government has in mind. All we have learned is that the Minister says that any money raised via the fund will not diminish the allocation to the department through Parliament. That should be "will not diminish an already diminished allocation" because we all know of the cut-backs which have already occurred in the Department of the Environment. There is, however, no assurance from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) or Treasury officials that we will see no further diminishing of the Parks Canada budget. That is not much of a guarantee at all.
The Minister says that the money will be used for special projects and not regular operations. The Bill itself is ambiguous on that point and offers no definition of "enhancing the park and site system". Furthermore, there will not be an arm's length agency to administer the fund. It will be at the Minister's discretion.
Where I come from and where the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior comes from this is called a slush fund and is suspect. I appreciate that the Member for Cochrane- Superior brought his vast experience with slush funds to bear on this debate and that he has now repented of his association with slush funds through his membership in the Liberal Party and a new day has dawned in the Liberal Party.
In any event, being enshrined in this Bill is a ministerial slush fund of which we are critical. We feel that it is an irresponsible and dangerous measure. It is irresponsible because there is already a mechanism for Canadians to make gifts to the Crown. The Minister says he wants to make it easier for Canadians to give lands and estates for parks. In effect, what he wants is a way to circumvent the Financial Administration Act.
Such a fund is dangerous because it is government encroachment on private fund-raising which already exists or may exist in the future. It would increase the moneys which are spent at the Minister's discretion, and it would consequently increase the leverage the Minister has over non-governmental organizations and other organizations which would be in line for grants flowing from this fund.
It is sad to note that some environmental groups have supported the notion of this fund. They are entitled to their view, but we feel that they have perhaps been influenced by the Minister's officials who have told them that this is the only way in which money can be made available for park projects. It is a sad commentary that this Minister sees more hope in getting money to enhance and expand his department's operations through voluntary taxation than through Treasury Board.
We in the New Democratic Party are not prepared to accept that we are at the limit of what Canadians are willing to spend on the preservation of their natural heritage. Obviously the Minister feels that we have reached that limit and that he must arrange a fund through which he can raid the moneys that might be available to other voluntary groups which are concerned about the environment.
Bill C-30 permits the Government to set boundaries for Banff and Jasper. The Government offers two reasons why it wants these boundaries to be legislated. It says that boundaries are needed before local self-government can be negotiated and that it wants to limit the development of town sites. Yet, we are not offered any idea of what these boundaries will be. By passing Bill C-30 Parliament may be agreeing to boundaries far wider than it would desire. We are basically asked to sign a blank cheque, to turn over the question of what boundaries may be established for Banff and Jasper to the Government. That is something we are not willing to do.
By the way, I understand that the citizens of Jasper have already indicated that they do not wish to pursue selfgovernment at this time. Residents of Banff, however, will be voting later this year on whether they wish to negotiate selfgovernment. I know that there are people in Alberta, who are looking to a different kind of self-government. They would like self-government for Alberta and I understand that some of them will be running against the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and other incumbents in Alberta.
I take it that the movement for self-government has really got off the ground in Alberta. That which is happening in the town site of Banff is only a manifestation of a larger phenomenon. We hope that this will not develop into a political movement which will sweep away the goon squad because we value them so highly. Besides, what would be the point of replacing the current goon squad with a separatist goon squad? We intend to sweep away the Alberta goon squad and replace them with New Democrats. That is the solution which we see to that problem.
April 15, 1988

Another issue in Bill C-30 is the definition and limitation of a ski area. Bill C-30 very explicitly states the exact boundaries of permitted ski resorts and places a moratorium on future ski development in the parks. There are currently five ski areas in national parks and a sixth is provided for by the federal-provincial arrangement which established Gros Morne National Park in Newfoundland.
It has been government policy for some years to limit the development of ski areas. This policy has not, unfortunately, been rigorously implemented and ski resorts have continued to expand, particularly in Banff National Park. There is a clear need to legislate boundaries for ski development and we welcome this provision of the Bill.
However, the Minister has already expressed his willingness to entertain changes to this section of Bill C-30. We know why. We know that it is because of the pressure applied on the Minister by the goon squad in Alberta with respect to a particular development in one of the national parks, the Sunshine ski hill. The Minister has said that it is okay with him if the committee studying the Bill decides to defer a decision on the Sunshine ski hill to some future date. Sunshine is remarkably successful, it seems, at getting Parks Canada to bend its policies and, although I really hope I am wrong in this, it seems to have won another round with the Minister.
I see that the Member for Ottawa-Carleton is shaking his head. I hope he is right. Time will tell. I know that the commitment of the Member for Ottawa-Carleton to this and to holding the line against the goon squad is beyond question and I wish him very well. He knows that he will have our support in this. We hope that the Minister has not been weakening on this matter of defining and living in ski areas.
Bill C-30 permits the Government to establish wilderness areas. It then requires the Minister not to authorize any activities which are likely to impair the wilderness character of the area. Notwithstanding this prohibition, Parks Canada can build rudimentary camp sites and permit aircraft to fly in.
One of the more striking deficiencies of Bill C-30 is a missing definition of wilderness. I admit that there might be some difficulty in defining wilderness, but no attempt is even made. We can infer from the activities which will be permitted that to Parks Canada wilderness is an area in which humans can camp, walk, travel by aircraft, and carry on other activities. Many Canadians would disagree with this definition. Many Canadians would say that there ought to be some wilderness which is in fact wilderness and left completely alone.
They would see wilderness as an area to be protected from human activity. Nowhere does Bill C-30 make any legislative provision for true wilderness sanctuaries. We see this as a serious shortcoming. For example, some members of the Alberta caucus-the same group to which I have been referring all along-are concerned that this Bill will stop the
National Parks Act
proposed condominium development at Maligne Lake. This is because Maligne Lake is apparently slated to be a wilderness area. However, Maligne Lake already has a small group of buildings at one end and motorboats, including tourist boats, on the lake. That is not my definition of wilderness. I hope it is not a definition which anyone else accepts.
One end of the lake is zoned for development and a corridor down the lake is zoned for commercial activities so that a diesel boat can travel back and forth on the lake. The sides of the lake are wilderness zones. I suggest we need a better zoning program for wilderness areas than is currently offered. It is as ridiculous as suggesting that if there is no housing in the bush at the edge of an airport, the area is a wilderness zone.
Maybe the bottom of the lake is wilderness.

Indeed. I would suggest that the wilderness might exist in the minds of the Alberta Tory caucus, but that would be an insult to wilderness. Before this Bill goes to committee the Minister should provide all interested Members with his plans for the zoning and preservation of a wilderness area.
Bill C-30 permits certain subsistence activities. For example, it permits the Minister to allow certain subsistence hunting and fishing and other activities in national parks when these are part of a federal-provincial agreement. We are in favour of this in principle, especially because we wish to see future parks developed in areas which are traditional hunting grounds for local peoples, particularly aboriginal peoples. The fact is that some of the new parks which we want to create are also the traditional lands of various aboriginal peoples. Some accommodation will have to be made between their rights and the desire of Canadians to establish national parks in these areas.
Those kinds of arrangements are being worked out, as in the case of South Moresby, and those kinds of arrangements will have to be worked out in future parks development where there is legitimate conflict between aboriginal rights and the desire of Canadians to establish national parks. The Government has given very little indication of its intentions in this area, and we want to see more detail.
To its credit, Bill C-30 accomplishes much housekeeping. Most of the amendments are to the regulatory power for parks administration and, generally speaking, we favour good housekeeping. Some of the proposed changes are disconcerting. For instance, the Government wishes to continue to be able to kill "dangerous or superabundant animals". The parks mandate is to permit natural processes to prevail. Therefore, is not the killing of superabundant animals against this philosophy? Likewise, permitting the destruction of dangerous animals denies what is often the reality of humans encroaching on the wildlife habitat of a park and putting these animals under the kind of pressure that results in attacks from time to time. This accepts the premise that it is appropriate to destroy

April 15, 1988
National Parks Act
animals which are disturbed in this way. We question that rationale.
The Bill expands the activities which may exist outside of town sites in national parks to include those for accommodation, recreation or entertainment of visitors to the parks. Courtesy of Bill C-30, the Government could permit a casino or amusement park to be built anywhere in the national parks system.
Bill C-30 authorizes regulated use of pesticides and other toxic substances in the parks. We believe that is something which should have been dealt with much more stringently.
In closing, I believe I have dealt with most of the NDP views on this Bill. We have no desire to delay it, but we want to have an adequate debate at second reading. I know that the environment critic for the New Democratic Party, the Elon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood will regret that she was not here. No notice was given that this Bill might be debated, and if the Government thinks it will play these kinds of games with important legislation like this and slip it through by surprise, it has another thought coming. We have others who are willing to speak to this Bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Hawkes (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to make a few comments about Bill C-30. First, I think I must deal with the closing comments of my hon. friend. He said that they have no desire to delay the legislation because it is important.
Four minutes prior to that he said it was his Party's position that the Bill could not even go forward to committee, where democracy could take place, until the Minister provided him with detailed zoning regulations for every national park in Canada. That is blackmail. It is the kind of blackmail that we have seen consistently with each piece of legislation that has come to this House this week. For five days we debated the joining of two Crown corporations into a stronger entity to enable it to compete better and provide more jobs. There were $3 million or $4 million in public funds expended on a piece of legislation so that those Members would be able to stand up in the future to say the Government cannot manage to get legislation through the House and we do not have time to deal with important issues.
