PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA SAFE DRINKING WATER ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-224, an Act to protect and enhance the quality of drinking water in Canada, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to say a few words on this Private Member's Bill that I put forward for the second time in this Parliament. The intention of the Bill is to attempt to address some of the serious concerns felt by Canadians about the quality of drinking water where they live. The Bill goes even further than that, and I will expand as I make my remarks this afternoon.
The explanation of the Bill itself is that it would protect and enhance the quality of drinking water in Canada. It provides for opportunities for public involvement in the making of regulations to set maximal permissible levels for contaminants and other substances in drinking water. The regulations would apply to both public and private water systems. The operator of a public water system would be required to monitor water quality regularly and supply the results to the users and to the Minister of the Environment. Any user of a private water system may have the water tested by the Minister of the Environment. Under this Bill, it would also be an offence for the operator of a public water system to provide water which contravenes the regulations or fails to comply with monitoring and notice requirements. It would also be an offence for anyone to pollute a public or private water system. The Bill also permits water users to sue or to recover damages for contraventions of the Act. It gives any person standing to seek judicial review against the Minister of the Environment. The Bill authorizes the Minister to commission research into matters related to drinking water quality and establish an advisory council to assist the Minister. That then is the explanation of the Bill.
During the last election campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised:
A P.C. Government will work with the provincial Governments to establish a set of regulations which will lead to standards for safe drinking water. This will be accomplished with due regard to the best practical technology and to economic constraints.
That promise was made by the Prime Minister during the last election campaign. The last time that the House had an opportunity to debate this Bill on January 21, 1985, the government Members' argument against having the Bill referred to a legislative committee at that time was that the Government had indeed made a commitment to do something about bringing in a safe drinking water Act. That was in January, 1985, and we still have not seen any indication from the Government that we are about to be presented with a safe drinking water Act. Some time ago in a paper tabled in the House, the Minister of the Environment also indicated that he would support bringing in such an Act.
In the absence of the Government coming forward with a proposed Act as has been promised, and assurances given to Canadians, the House is now given the opportunity to deal with this important matter and, indeed, refer it to a legislative committee for public input, discussion, and to allow Members on all sides of the House to examine the importance of this question. Since January, 1985, the House has not had an opportunity to express its views on this question. That is one of the reasons why the House of Commons committee that makes recommendations on Private Members' Business did recommend that this Bill be given some priority for debate in the House. That is why it is here again today.
In terms of the debate it is useful to take a look at some of the information that we do have about the quality of drinking water, not only in Canada but elsewhere. While Canada has less than 1 per cent of the world's population, we possess an estimated 25 per cent of the earth's fresh water. The Great Lakes contain 18 per cent of the planet's surface fresh water. Canada's rivers have a combined flow of 68,000 cubic metres per second, enough to fill all of the country's bathtubs every 10 seconds. On a global scale, fresh water constitutes only 0.2 per cent of the total water supply.
Until the first decades of the 20th century, water-borne diseases such as typhoid fever claimed the lives of many Canadians. Although modern medicine has advanced to the point where this disease is no longer a serious threat, new forms of water-borne diseases are still emerging. The World Health Organization indicates that in the Third World diseases associated with dirty water kills 50,000 people every day, more than 80 million people per year. As long as bacterial contamination of Canadian water is allowed to continue, such as that generated by food processing plants, Canadians cannot assume that they are immune to water-borne diseases that currently plague the Third World.
Currently the greatest threat to Canada's drinking water is caused by chemical contaminants. It has been estimated by many environmental scientists, including those associated with
April 15, 1988

the federal Department of the Environment that, in the Great Lakes alone, there are anywhere between 400 and 800 known chemicals which have been identified in the Great Lakes waters. Among those existing pollutants are mercury, lead, copper, chromium, zinc, PAHs (polyaromatic hydrocarbons), phenols, asbestos fibres, arsenic, PCBs, DDT, chlorinated organics, dioxin, HCB (hevachlorobenzene), ammonia, mirex and selenium.
Most of those chemicals come from a variety of sources, but one of the worst areas of concern are those chemical plants located on the U.S. side of the Niagara River. Approximately four or five years ago I had an opportunity to go to the Niagara Peninsula and over to the New York side of the Niagara River and take a look at some of those chemical companies which operate there. Some of the most serious environmental problems are coming from these chemical plants and on dump sites which, when one takes a look at the map of the U.S. side of the Niagara River, enough to scare one half to death when one notices how close those chemical dump sites are located to the face of the Niagara gorge. I will return to that in a second.
Some of the best known sources of pollution over there are the infamous Love Canal, the Hyde Park dump site, the "S" area dump, the 102nd Street dump, and the Niagara Falls, New York, Waste Water Treatment Plant, among many others.
It is worth-while pointing out that I was the chairman of this particular group that went there to take a look at this. I received agreement from all Parties in the House to table the report that we had drawn up as a result of that investigation. Certainly, the Members who were in the House at that time and who gave agreement to the tabling of the report, recognized the seriousness of the situation. What happened and is still happening is that when those chemical companies wanted to get rid of waste, all they did was excavate large holes in the ground and dumped these waste chemicals in there willy-nilly. They were dumped in a raw state without any kind of pretreatment. They were put in containers which were bound to leak and leach in later years, and that is exactly what is happening. As the chemicals are freed from the containers, they are going into ground water supplies and through the ground water into the Niagara River.
In fact, when we visited the area, coincidentally the CTV Television Network also had a camera crew down there which took an aquarium tank and filled it with water from the Niagara River. Then they placed a live fish in the tank. I am sure it was just coincidence but the fish immediately jumped out of the tank, even though scientific data indicate that the Niagara River is so polluted now that scientists can hardly even measure how much fresh water is in that river.
It is a very serious matter. Much of the pollutants which have gone into the Niagara River have been in the form of
Canada Safe Drinking Water Act
dioxin, the dioxin used in the Vietnam war to defoliate trees. That was the initial intention, but of course we know what it did to human beings.
I believe it was a scientist working for Environment Canada who estimated that one shovel full of dioxin thrown into the Great Lakes would kill anything that lived in the Great Lakes for the next 100 years. However, we have chemical dump sites on the U.S. side of the Niagara River containing tonnes of this stuff. It is leaching into the river and posing a very serious threat to the drinking water supply of some six million Canadians who live around Lake Ontario, not least of whom are those who happen to live in my constituency of Beaches located right on the edge of Lake Ontario.
The Government's response-and I am sure that we will hear it in this debate as well-to this kind of alarming report is that all it serves to do is to scare Canadians.
As a result of the last time that I spoke on the matter in the House, I received a number of telephone calls from people in my constituency who happened to be pregnant. They asked: "Should I be drinking water from Lake Ontario?" It is an extremely difficult question to answer. I drink the water myself, but it is absolutely clear that doctors and scientists recommend that pregnant women not eat any more than one fish per year caught in Lake Ontario. Just as a matter of interest, when I first heard that recommendation a number of years ago, I asked the then Minister of National Health and Welfare in the previous Liberal Government why the allowable dioxin contamination in fish happened to be 20 parts per trillion in Canada while in the United States the limit was 10 parts per trillion.
The response I received was that it was twice as much in Canada because Canadians ate half as much fish on a per capita basis as did Americans. In other words, the Government's response to that contamination in fish was that because we eat half as much fish as Americans supposedly do, our bodies can absorb twice as much dioxin. My answer to that was that if one eats more than the average amount of fish for a Canadian, one is out of luck; one is really out of luck.
This is the kind of response that we have been receiving from Governments. They indicate that all we are trying to do is scare people and that the trace amounts of all the contaminants I have mentioned, including dioxin, in the Great Lakes are in such minute quantities that it is inconceivable that they would present any kind of danger to anyone's health.
I should like to dispute that point, because it has been estimated that anywhere between 400 and 800 known, identifiable chemicals have been found in the Great Lakes. No one knows what effect each of these chemicals have on each other. Even although they may be in minute traces, by the time they combine with each other they may well be establishing some new kind of chemical. This was pointed out in an issue of Protect Yourself magazine on Canada's drinking water, wherein an environmental scientist indicated the following:

April 15, 1988
Canada Safe Drinking Water Act
While it is true that the Great Lakes may contain up to 800 known chemicals, and any number of unknown substances, it is also true that chemical levels are extremely low. The development of sophisticated technology in the past two decades has enabled scientists to detect minute quantities of substances in our water supply.
Dioxin, for example, can be measured in parts per quadrillion. The current measurement standard is parts per billion ... We have almost reached the stage where we are measuring numbers of molecules. Yet as Dr. Ross Hall, a professor of biochemistry at McMaster University, has pointed out, to a human cell, "a part per trillion is not a minute amount... It represents a few hundred molecules. And we know in the case of dioxin that a few hundred molecules is sufficient to impact on a cell harmfully." So the fact that chemical levels in drinking water are very low should not induce complacency. Once again, it is important to keep in mind that there is a great deal we don't know about the effects of modern pollutants. Much more research is needed, for example, on the phenomenon of chemical synergism, or interaction.
Synergism is the process whereby two or more substances, acting together, have a combined effect that is greater than the sum of their individual effects. This process is well-illustrated by the medical histories of workers in asbestos industry. The incidence of cancer amongst asbestos workers is nine times higher than it is amongst the general population. Yet the risk of cancer is 92 times higher amongst asbestos workers who smoke, in comparison to the rate amongst men who neither smoke nor work with asbestos.
That is just a very simple example of some of the scientific concerns which have been expressed about the lack of government action in the whole area of water quality.
In that my time has practically expired, I want to wind up by saying very seriously that the only standards which exist in Canada for the safe drinking water supply have nothing to do with human beings. The only standards which exist at the present time concern fish. If one poisons a fish by contaminating water, one is liable to charges under existing regulations. However, there is nothing to say that one cannot pollute drinking water or any kind of water to endanger human beings; it is only if it endangers fish.
I have called time and time again to have the matter referred to a standing committee of the House to allow Hon. Members to examine the matter in a much closer way than we can examine it by considering a Private Member's Bill for one hour, to call expert testimony, and to listen to and give the public an opportunity to express its concerns about the quality of drinking water in Canadian communities. I think the House would serve those people very well if it were to give them that kind of opportunity.
I say seriously to Hon. Members on all sides of the House: "Don't talk this Bill out, refer it to a legislative committee, and allow for the kind of discussion this matter of serious consequence deserves".

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA SAFE DRINKING WATER ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak today about safe drinking water, an issue of vital importance to the health and well-being of all Canadians, and one that is particularly by important to the Department of National Health and Welfare. I am indeed much encouraged by the initiative taken by the Hon. Member for
Beaches (Mr. Young) in tabling Bill C-224 which concerns safe drinking water. This Bill is similar to Bills C-212, C-226 and C-276 that were tabled in the past three years.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has stressed many times how vital safe drinking water is to public health, and that is why, as was pointed out by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), the Department of National Health and Welfare is primarily responsible at the federal level for the quality of our drinking water.
When similar legislation, C-212, C-266 and C-276, was introduced previously, we indicated at the time that the Government intended to introduce legislation on safe drinking water in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that both levels of government, federal and provincial or territorial, have an important role to play in the distribution of safe drinking water. The Department of National Health and Welfare of course appreciates the fact that provincial governments have always taken responsibility for the treatment of water for the purposes of production and distribution of drinking water. While the provinces are primarily responsible for the protection and control of drinking water supplies, authority is generally delegated to municipalities and public utilities for the production and distribution of drinking water in their respective communities. The standards or guidelines to be met are defined by the Department of National Health and Welfare, in co-operation with the provincial goverments.
As a matter of fact, the Department has been actively involved in setting standards for the quality of drinking water since 1923, when an order in council was adopted to regulate the bacteriological content of drinking water on board ships using continental water supplies. In 1968, the Department published the first set of universal standards and objectives for drinking water in Canada, prescribing standards for a substantial number of toxic chemicals and also for radioactive substances and microorganisms. These standards were completely revised in 1978 by a joint federal-provincial committee, which produced recommendations for the quality of drinking water in Canada, including guidelines on fifty-one parameters, of which forty-two involved chemical substances.
Since that time, Mr. Speaker, new scientific data have found that water contains a broad range of chemical products and that some of them enter the water as a result of the treatment process itself. Considering this new information, the Department has recognized the need for revising its recommendations for the quality of drinking water in Canada, and this document is now in the process of being published. As in the past, the review process took place with the full co-operation and participation of the provincial governments, under the auspices of the Joint Federal-Provincial Advisory Board on Environmental and Occupational Health. Considering the importance of the safety of our drinking water and the rapidly increasing body of knowledge in this respect, a standing sub-committee has been set up so that we can update the recommendations on
April 15, 1988

an on-going basis and also consider other important matters related to water supplies generally. In fact, the actual changes are already being made.
The next edition of the recommendations will include 41 pesticides, of which 31 were not previously considered. The recommendations will include 15 new organic parameters and the re-evaluation of nine inorganic and organic substances, including an evaluation of the need to set guidelines for PCBs and dioxins, which interest and concern many Canadians now.
Setting guidelines is not the only activity related to drinking water that the Department of National Health and Welfare carries out. The safety of drinking water supplies can only be assured with a much broader approach. Overall, the Department's long-term goals for drinking water are:
-Ensure that all Canadians are supplied with drinking water that satisfies the recommendations for drinking water quality in Canada;
-Ensure that the operational safety of point-of-use water treatment devices sold commercially is determined by laboratory tests under actual conditions, so that potentially dangerous devices are removed from the market;
-Ensure also that all chemicals and materials directly or indirectly involved in the production, distribution or conservation of drinking water be evaluated for their potential dangers in order to guarantee their safety.
Mr. Speaker, in view of the concerns expressed about the quality of some drinking water, it seems that some Canadians have lost confidence in their municipal drinking water to the extent that they turn to other sources of supply or feel obliged to further purify their own drinking water. It is estimated that the sales of bottled water made by the soft drink industry alone amount to some $15 million a year. Spring water and other types of water sold in containers can be seen on the shelves of grocery stores and pharmacies and sometimes even at roadside stands.
Over the last few years, we have also witnessed a proliferation of devices of every imaginable kind to treat water at the point of use and it seems that these devices are increasingly popular with the general public. Departmental surveys carried out in major Canadian cities indicate that about 3 per cent of all households are using some device to treat tap water and that half of these devices are equipped with activated charcoal filters. Beside their prices, most of the devices available in stores have one or several other use-related inconveniences, so that any improvement perceived in the water quality could in fact go hand in hand with a number of potential hazards.
It is important to remember that the treatment of drinking water to make it safe and its subsequent distribution to consumers could also contribute to the contamination process. Many products may be used to treat water, including disinfectants, coagulants, dechlorination agents, fluoridation and fluoride adjustment agents, as well as corrosion and scale prevention compounds, and water softeners. Among the
Canada Safe Drinking Water Act
materials used in the building of water storage and distribution system pipes and liners, we could single out cement coated cast iron and steel, asbestos cement, plastics (for instance, polyvinyl chloride, polybutylene, chlorinated polyethylene), epoxy resins, enamels, as well as tar pitch and bituminous mastics.
As a rule, Mr. Speaker, when these products are prepared for a drinking water related application, they are of higher quality. Just the same, it would be appropriate to set up strict standards to assess the health acceptability of all products and chemical substances in contact with drinking water; the possibilities for implementation of appropriate measures are under active study by the Department of National Health and Welfare and some provincial organizations.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that even though the principle underlying Bill C-224 is commendable, the Department believes that it fails to address the whole series of questions which must be considered so that we can continue to have a reliable supply of safe drinking water. In addition, it does not really take into full consideration the major role played by the provinces in this field. Any new legislation in this field simply must include provisions to harmonize the respective roles of the provinces and of the federal Government. Obviously a new and specific parliamentary mandate must be established if the quality and safety of Canada's drinking water supply are to be guaranteed. Legislation does exist, but it does not cover new issues, including the one to which I have just alluded. The only requirements pertaining to drinking water in the regulations adopted pursuant to the Department of National Health and Welfare Act concern public transport companies. The Food and Drugs Act does give specific powers but, except for bottled water, they are not exercised because the executory powers are quite inappropriate in the case of collective drinking water supplies.
In this respect, in recent months, representatives of the Department of National Health and Welfare have been meeting with the interested parties, including spokesmen for the provinces, concerning the possibility of extending the powers of the federal government to monitor the quality of drinking water.
Mr. Speaker, I think that what I have just said clearly indicates that the Department of National Health and Welfare is committed to see to it that Canadians can indeed count on reliable water supplies and that, in co-operation with the other parties involved, we are seriously considering measures which will enable us to reach that goal.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have an opportunity to put forward some comments on Bill C-224 proposed by my friend, the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young).
Safe drinking water is one of the basic requirements for good health and is therefore of great importance not only to all Canadians but also to the Department of National Health and Welfare. The department is pleased to observe the widespread interest and concern over the issue of safe drinking water, particularly with the introduction of this Bill and Bill C-266 and Bill C-276.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) has noted that primary responsibility for drinking water quality at the federal level lies with the Department of National Health and Welfare. This is for a number of reasons. Water is, first, a basic necessity of life. Our bodies cannot function without it. It is also the basis of good personal and domestic hygiene which is essential to prevent the spread of many diseases. Water may
Canada Safe Drinking Water Act
also have a beneficial effect in preventing or reducing the incidence of disease. For example, the association between water hardness and a reduction in the incidence of cardiovascular disease, and a highly significant reduction in dental decay owing to the presence of fluoride in drinking water.
However, water can also have an adverse effect on health and this is our concern today. It can carry micro-organisms that cause diseases such as typhoid and cholera. Human beings can also be exposed to many types of toxic substances which find their way into water, such as chlorinated hydrocarbons and pesticides, heavy metals such as lead, mercury and arsenic, and inorganic chemicals such as nitrates and radionuclides. I should mention here that the department was at the forefront in providing advice on the increased levels of radioactive chemicals in water which resulted from the radioactive fall-out from the Chernobyl nuclear accident in 1986.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has specific powers relating to drinking water under the Food and Drugs Act. Although regulations have been established for bottled water and pre-packaged ice, the department has so far chosen not to use the powers conferred by this legislation to control public community water supplies. This decision was made because of the traditional arrangements whereby provinces have the primary responsibility to protect and control drinking water resources from which potable water supplies are produced.
Notwithstanding this, however, the department developed guidelines to protect against adverse effects of contaminants in drinking water and to minimize unpleasant aesthetic characteristics of water. This was accomplished with the full cooperation and participation of the provincial and territorial Governments, under the federal-provincial Advisory Committee on Environmental and Occupational Health. The department's first comprehensive drinking water standards and objectives were developed in 1968, and later revised in 1978 by a joint federal-provincial mechanism.
The 1978 guidelines have served us well, but the scientific data base from which they are derived is constantly changing. The department recognized the need to revise the Canadian drinking water guidelines, and the 1987 edition of the revised guidelines is now in publication. Once again, the revisions were accomplished through a federal-provincial mechanism.
Because of the importance of safe drinking water and the rapid advances in scientific data, a permanent subcommittee has been established to update guidelines and deal with important issues related to drinking water supply.
The department plays an active role in many areas pertaining to drinking water quality. It has initiated biannual national conferences on drinking water, the first of which was held in Ottawa in 1984. These conferences are co-sponsored by a number of agencies or organizations which have an interest in water quality. The second conference held in Edmonton in 1986 focused on an issue of concern to scientists and lay people alike. The topic was "Treatment for Organic Contaminants".

The next conference is scheduled for St. John's, Newfoundland, on the topic of "Small System Alternatives".
Health and Welfare Canada is also involved in a wide range of research projects such as conducting studies to ascertain whether asbestos ingested from drinking water can cause cancer, and collaboration with the Province of New Brunswick in a study to determine if there is any association between nitrate in drinking water and birth defects. Here in Ontario the Ministry of the Environment and the Department of National Health and Welfare have jointly funded a study carried out by the Canadian Public Health Association on the impact of chemicals in the Great Lakes on drinking water quality.
Another area of interest is the effect acid rain may have on drinking water quality. Departmental officials have already conducted a survey on water quality in rural areas and cottages around Muskoka. Model studies are being conducted at present at La Ronge, Saskatchewan, Sioux Lookout, Ontario, in the Canadian Shield, and in Shelburne, Nova Scotia. The aim is to develop an index that will help identify drinking water supplies being affected by acid rain. In addition, the department has ongoing research programs to control disease-causing micro-organisms in drinking water more effectively. It is collaborating with research centres conducting studies on the intestinal parasite Giardia Lamblia, which is the organism responsible for most water-borne diseases in Canada.
The Canadian public is increasingly concerned about the adequacy of conventional water treatment processes and some have purchased their own treatment devices to address the problem. A recent survey conducted by the department in metropolitan centres in Canada found that some kind of device is used in about 3 per cent of homes to treat municipal water supplies. Activated carbon filters are the most common devices on the market. Although they are relatively effective in removing chlorine, organic chemicals, taste and odour, one disadvantage is the growth of bacteria on the filter medium. Most devices have one or more drawbacks associated with their use. The department evaluates and, in some cases, tests devices and provides advice to consumers, other federal departments, provincial Governments and some agencies.
No Bill regarding safe water would be complete without addressing the piping and lining materials used in water storage and distribution systems since these materials can also add contaminants to the water. It is imperative that any new legislation include mechanisms to evaluate, from a health point of view, the acceptability of all products and chemicals used in contact with potable water.
Bill C-224 has many positive elements but does not recognize the vital role of the Minister of the Department of National Health and Welfare regarding drinking water and does not acknowledge the function of the provinces in this
area. It is very clear that new legislation is needed to assure the quality and safety of drinking water supplies in Canada. However, such legislation must address all the issues. Consultation with the provinces will continue and efforts will be made to provide all Canadians with drinking water of the highest possible quality.

Mr. Speaker, I rise as a committed environmentalist to speak on what I consider to be one of the most important environmental questions in Canada, perhaps in the world, that is, the issue of plentiful, clean, fresh drinking water.
In 1745 Benjamin Franklin, a noted American said: "When the well is dry we know the worth of water". Most Canadians feel that we in Canada are awash with water and that the well will never be dry. After all, Canada has less than 1 per cent of the world's population yet possesses an estimated 25 per cent of the earth's fresh water. The Great Lakes contain 18 per cent of the planet's surface fresh water and Canada's rivers have a combined flow of 68,000 cubic metres per second, enough to fill all the country's bathtubs every 10 seconds. Yet, on a global scale fresh water constitutes only 0.2 per cent of the total water supply. That reminds me of the line in Coleridge's Ancient Mariner.
Water, water, everywhere,
Nor any drop to drink.
Water, water, everywhere,
And still the ship did sink.
The ship may be analagous to the world in which we have a tremendous need for fresh water. We have the fresh water in Canada and the question is whether we are going to preserve it. That is why this Bill before us is very important.
This Bill provides opportunities for public involvement in the making of regulations to set maximum permissible levels for contaminants in drinking water. It calls for the establishment of a water review board which would be empowered to hold hearings on the safety of our drinking water. The Bill also calls for a water advisory council which would advise the Minister of the Environment as to the results of current research related to drinking water quality.
The operator of a public water system would be required to monitor water quality regularly and notify the users of the system as well as the Minister of the Environment of the results in order that people would know about their systems. Any use of a private water system could have the water tested by the Minister of the Environment.
Under the proposed Act it would be an offence for the operator of a public water system to provide water which contravenes the regulations or fails to comply with monitoring and notice requirements. It would be an offence for anyone to pollute a public or private water system as is happening in many places in Canada now.

The Bill would permit water users to sue to recover damages for contraventions of the Act which would give it some teeth. Any person could seek judicial review against the Minister of the Environment under this proposed legislation in order that he or she would be forced to do his job. This is a good Bill.
In the new riding which I hope to represent in the next Parliament, Port Moody-Coquitlam, the municipalities of Belcarra, Port Moody, Port Coquitlam, and Coquitlam are located on the other side of Simon Fraser University where there are rolling hills and a view to the North Shore mountains which is unsurpassed. When you look at those North Shore mountains and see the beauty, the trees, and the snow at the top, you think that we have water forever. However, the fact is that we do not necessarily have water forever. We must ensure that that water is protected.
I started out as an environmentalist because I was counsel to the Berger inquiry on the Mackenzie Valley pipeline about 15 years ago. That was a great inquiry because it studied the environmental impact of a large project in northern Canada. We blazed new ground in studying that project and I became a very committed environmentalist.
Justice Tom Berger said an interesting thing when addressing an audience in Toronto. He said that Canadians are northerners, that Canadians are environmentalists, and that every part of the country belongs to everyone in the country. People in Toronto have an interest in the North and in the clean water and beautiful environment of British Columbia. We in British Columbia and those people in the North have an interest in helping the people of Toronto to make their drinking water pure as well.
We are a northern country, we are a northern people. We are a people very attuned to the environment. Canadians love their environment and are committed environmentalists. It is not good enough in this debate today to hear from two spokespersons for the government departments. Ordinary Members of Parliament should be pushing for this Bill as well.
On May 2, 1980,1 stood in this House and introduced a Bill entitled an Act respecting a national park on Moresby Island and its adjacent islands. There were a lot of people pressing for this. I had help from the Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), the Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), and the present Minister of the Environment. Many people worked together. The Government in my province had to be brought aboard kicking and screaming. It would prefer to mine in provincial parks. However, together we achieved a national park in South Moresby.
Like South Moresby, the time for this Bill on clean drinking water will come too. The Government and Canadians will realize that although we have an abundance of water resources

in this country we will want to preserve those resources through a clean water Act.
There are other water issues. There are a couple of schemes now to export water from Canada. There is a scheme to damn up the Rocky Mountain trench and send water to the United States via that route. There is another scheme to damn up James Bay and make it a fresh water lake. The people involved in that scheme are not unknown, this is not science fiction. They include Simon Reisman, Robert Bourassa, and others.
There is an issue of water exports, an issue of safe water, and an issue of clean water. That is why I am very proud to support this Bill today. Its time I hope will soon come to be enacted into legislation.

We saw in the paper this morning that there are fish full of tumours in the Niagara River. This is unbelievable. The Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) cited: "Water, water everywhere, And all the boards did shrink". The only thing that is shrinking in this country is our access to good fresh water. One of the areas in which that is happening is right here in the national capital region in the Rideau River and Mooney's Bay.
I see the Member for Beaches. When I hear the word "beaches" I think of sand, of beaches, and of Mooney's Bay. The fact is that if you fall out of your boat into that piece of water in August they will rush you to the Riverside Hospital for a tetanus shot because it is so polluted that if you swallow any of it you will die. The Government must act to clean up our water.
